items.signText:
Tom – the printer on our floor has broken down again and the engineer can't come until Thursday. Until then, please use the one on the second floor, but remember it only prints in black and white.
Priya
items.question: Why has Priya written to Tom?
options: a) To warn him that colour printing is no longer possible in the office
b) To tell him where he can print until the printer is repaired
c) To ask him to contact the engineer before Thursday
items.explanation: Priya writes 'Until then, please use the one on the second floor', so she is telling Tom which printer to use until the engineer comes. She does not ask him to contact the engineer, and she only says the second-floor printer is black and white, not that colour printing is impossible for good.

items.signText:
Jack – Mr Evans from Greenfield Ltd phoned at 10.30. He can't come to this afternoon's meeting and would like to move it to tomorrow at the same time. Could you call him back to confirm?
Sam
items.question: What does Jack need to do?
options: a) Phone Mr Evans to confirm the new meeting time
b) Tell Mr Evans that the meeting will start later this afternoon
c) Wait for Mr Evans to phone again later today
items.explanation: Sam writes 'Could you call him back to confirm?' after explaining that Mr Evans wants to move the meeting to tomorrow at the same time. So Jack must phone Mr Evans; he is not asked to wait for another call, and the meeting is moving to tomorrow, not starting later today.

items.signText:
To: All staff
From: Maria (IT)
The office Wi-Fi password is changing on Monday. Everyone will receive the new password by text message early on Monday morning. Please don't ask reception for it, as they won't have it.
items.question: How will staff get the new Wi-Fi password?
options: a) They will be sent it in a text message.
b) They can collect it from reception on Monday.
c) They have to choose a new one before Monday.
items.explanation: Maria writes 'Everyone will receive the new password by text message early on Monday morning'. She says reception 'won't have it', and staff do not choose the password themselves.

items.signText:
MEETING ROOM 3
This room is booked for the sales team every Tuesday from 9 to 11 a.m. If you need it at any other time, please write your name and the time on the list at reception, not on this door.
items.question: What does the notice say?
options: a) The sales team must write their names on the door of the room.
b) Anyone can use this room on Tuesday mornings if it is empty.
c) People who want the room at other times should book it at reception.
items.explanation: The notice says 'If you need it at any other time, please write your name and the time on the list at reception'. The room is booked for the sales team on Tuesday mornings, so it is not free for anyone then, and names should go on the reception list, 'not on this door'.

items.signText:
STAFF KITCHEN
The fridge will be cleaned on Friday at 4 p.m. Any food or drink without a name on it will be thrown away, but items with a name label can stay.
items.question: What should staff do?
options: a) Stay out of the kitchen while the fridge is being cleaned.
b) Clean the fridge themselves on Friday at 4 p.m.
c) Put a name label on any food they want to keep.
items.explanation: The notice says food 'without a name on it will be thrown away' and 'items with a name label can stay', so staff should label food they want to keep. The kitchen is not closed, and the notice says the fridge 'will be cleaned', not that staff must clean it.

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 3.
lesenParts.textTitle: The teenager who helped a whole street
lesenParts.text:
When sixteen-year-old Maya Collins started building an app in her bedroom two years ago, she had no idea that it would soon be used by more than fifty thousand people. 'Honestly, I just wanted to solve a problem in my own family,' she says.

The problem began one winter. Maya's grandmother slipped on some ice and broke her leg. She lived alone, and although Maya's parents visited as often as they could, they both worked long hours in another town. 'Gran's neighbours kept telling us they would happily help her with shopping or collecting medicine,' Maya explains. 'But they never knew when she actually needed something, and she was too proud to knock on their doors and ask.'

That gave Maya the idea for Next Door, an app which lets older people post small requests that neighbours nearby can accept with one click. There was only one difficulty: Maya had never written a line of computer code. She spent the next six months teaching herself from free online videos, often working until midnight at weekends. 'My first version was a disaster,' she laughs. 'It crashed every time more than two people used it at once.'

Help came from an unexpected place. Maya's computer science teacher, Mr Okafor, noticed her working on the app during a lunch break and offered to look at it with her. 'He didn't fix it for me,' she says. 'He just asked the right questions until I understood what I'd done wrong. That was much more useful.'

After a few more months of testing with her grandmother's neighbours, Maya put Next Door online. At first only a handful of families in her street joined, but then a local radio station interviewed her, and the number of users grew almost overnight. Today the app is used in towns all over the country.

Several companies have since offered to buy Next Door, but Maya has turned them all down. 'They wanted to add advertising and charge people to use it,' she says. 'The people who need it most are often the ones with the least money, so that's not going to happen.'

Maya admits it hasn't always been easy to balance the app with her schoolwork, especially during exams. She now spends only Sunday afternoons on it, and a small team of volunteers answers users' messages during the week.

Her advice for other young people with an idea is simple. 'Don't wait until you feel ready, because you never will. Start with something small, and expect it to go wrong. That's how you learn.'

questions.question: Why did Maya decide to create the app?
questions.explanation: Maya says the neighbours 'would happily help' but 'they never knew when she actually needed something'. Her grandmother did not ask for help at all – she was 'too proud to knock on their doors and ask' – so the neighbours never refused her.
options: a) Her grandmother had asked the neighbours for help and they had refused.
b) She wanted to enter a competition for young app designers.
c) Her parents asked her to find a way of looking after her grandmother.
d) Her grandmother's neighbours wanted to help but did not know when.

questions.question: What does Maya say about the first version of Next Door?
questions.explanation: Maya says 'It crashed every time more than two people used it at once'. She spent six months teaching herself, not a few weeks, and her teacher only helped her later, after he noticed her working on the app at lunch.
options: a) It stopped working as soon as a few people used it together.
b) It took her only a few weeks to build from online videos.
c) She built it with help from her teacher.
d) Her parents helped her to test it at weekends.

questions.question: How did Mr Okafor help Maya?
questions.explanation: Maya says 'He didn't fix it for me. He just asked the right questions until I understood what I'd done wrong.' She found the online videos herself, and he saw her working on the app during a lunch break, not in lessons.
options: a) He recommended some free online videos to her.
b) He let her work on the app during his lessons.
c) He asked her questions until she saw her own mistakes.
d) He corrected the problems in her code himself at lunch.

questions.question: Why has Maya refused to sell the app?
questions.explanation: The companies 'wanted to add advertising and charge people to use it', and Maya says 'The people who need it most are often the ones with the least money'. She does not mention the amount of money offered, and she does not want anyone to pay.
options: a) The companies did not offer her enough money.
b) She wants it to stay free for people who might not be able to pay.
c) She is worried that selling it would take up too much of her time.
d) She is planning to charge users for it herself.

questions.question: What advice does Maya give to young people with an idea?
questions.explanation: Maya says 'Start with something small, and expect it to go wrong. That's how you learn.' She also says 'Don't wait until you feel ready', which is the opposite of waiting until you have all the skills, and she sees mistakes as the way to learn rather than something to avoid.
options: a) Ask an expert to check your idea before you do anything.
b) Try hard to avoid making mistakes in the early stages.
c) Start small and accept that things will go wrong.
d) Wait until you have all the skills you need before starting.

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 4.
lesenParts.text:
Last June, my sister Clare and I decided to spend a week cycling along the coast of Cornwall, from Padstow to Penzance. Neither of us had any experience of cycling holidays, and we weren't particularly fit either. (1) ______ We simply thought it would be a cheap and healthy way to see a beautiful part of the country.

We hired our bikes from a small shop in Padstow. The owner, a friendly man called Pete, spent almost an hour checking that our seats were the right height and showing us how to fix a flat tyre. (2) ______ He also gave us a map with the quietest roads marked in red, which turned out to be extremely useful.

The first day was hard work. The coast road goes up and down constantly, and by lunchtime our legs were aching. (3) ______ Luckily, the views of the sea from the top of each hill made all the effort worthwhile, and by the evening we were already feeling stronger.

On the third morning, just outside the village of St Agnes, Clare's back tyre suddenly went flat. There was no bike shop for miles and hardly any traffic on the road. (4) ______ Twenty minutes later we were back on our bikes, feeling rather proud of ourselves.

Each night we stayed in a small guest house, which we had booked before we left home. (5) ______ Most of them were also happy to let us keep our bikes in their garden or garage overnight, and one even washed our muddy clothes for us.

By the time we reached Penzance, we had cycled nearly two hundred kilometres. We were tired, sunburnt and very happy, and we are already planning next year's trip.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (1)?
questions.explanation: The writer has just said they had no experience and 'weren't particularly fit'; 'In fact' explains that they did not choose the trip because they loved cycling, and the next sentence gives the real reason: 'We simply thought it would be a cheap and healthy way to see a beautiful part of the country'. The sentence about Clare having cycled the route before cannot fit, because the text says 'Neither of us had any experience'.
options: A) We had to get off and push our bikes up several of the steepest hills.
B) Clare, on the other hand, had cycled this route several times before.
C) The owners were always interested to hear where we had cycled that day.
D) In fact, we didn't choose this holiday because we loved cycling.
E) Because of this, we had to spend the rest of the week camping in a field.
F) Thanks to Pete's lesson, however, we were able to repair it ourselves.
G) At the time we thought this was unnecessary, but we were glad of it later.
H) We decided to take the train for the last part of the journey instead.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (2)?
questions.explanation: 'This' refers to Pete showing them 'how to fix a flat tyre', and 'we were glad of it later' prepares for the flat tyre on the third morning. The sentence about repairing the tyre cannot go here, because nothing has broken yet.
options: A) We had to get off and push our bikes up several of the steepest hills.
B) Clare, on the other hand, had cycled this route several times before.
C) The owners were always interested to hear where we had cycled that day.
D) In fact, we didn't choose this holiday because we loved cycling.
E) Because of this, we had to spend the rest of the week camping in a field.
F) Thanks to Pete's lesson, however, we were able to repair it ourselves.
G) At the time we thought this was unnecessary, but we were glad of it later.
H) We decided to take the train for the last part of the journey instead.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (3)?
questions.explanation: The road 'goes up and down constantly' and their legs were aching, so they had to push their bikes up 'the steepest hills'. The next sentence continues the idea: 'the views of the sea from the top of each hill made all the effort worthwhile'. Taking the train cannot fit, as they cycled all the way to Penzance.
options: A) We had to get off and push our bikes up several of the steepest hills.
B) Clare, on the other hand, had cycled this route several times before.
C) The owners were always interested to hear where we had cycled that day.
D) In fact, we didn't choose this holiday because we loved cycling.
E) Because of this, we had to spend the rest of the week camping in a field.
F) Thanks to Pete's lesson, however, we were able to repair it ourselves.
G) At the time we thought this was unnecessary, but we were glad of it later.
H) We decided to take the train for the last part of the journey instead.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (4)?
questions.explanation: There was 'no bike shop for miles', but 'however' shows a contrast: because Pete had taught them, they could 'repair it' (the flat tyre) themselves, and 'Twenty minutes later we were back on our bikes'. Camping in a field cannot fit, because they continued cycling and stayed in guest houses.
options: A) We had to get off and push our bikes up several of the steepest hills.
B) Clare, on the other hand, had cycled this route several times before.
C) The owners were always interested to hear where we had cycled that day.
D) In fact, we didn't choose this holiday because we loved cycling.
E) Because of this, we had to spend the rest of the week camping in a field.
F) Thanks to Pete's lesson, however, we were able to repair it ourselves.
G) At the time we thought this was unnecessary, but we were glad of it later.
H) We decided to take the train for the last part of the journey instead.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (5)?
questions.explanation: 'The owners' are the owners of the guest houses mentioned just before, and the next sentence, 'Most of them were also happy to let us keep our bikes…', continues describing them. Camping in a field contradicts the guest houses they had booked.
options: A) We had to get off and push our bikes up several of the steepest hills.
B) Clare, on the other hand, had cycled this route several times before.
C) The owners were always interested to hear where we had cycled that day.
D) In fact, we didn't choose this holiday because we loved cycling.
E) Because of this, we had to spend the rest of the week camping in a field.
F) Thanks to Pete's lesson, however, we were able to repair it ourselves.
G) At the time we thought this was unnecessary, but we were glad of it later.
H) We decided to take the train for the last part of the journey instead.

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 5.
lesenParts.text:
Most of us know we should eat more fruit and vegetables, but changing the way we eat is not always easy. Experts say the secret is to (1) ______ small changes, one at a time, rather than trying to change everything at once.

For example, instead of (2) ______ breakfast because you are in a hurry, try preparing something the night before. A bowl of porridge with some fresh fruit will (3) ______ you full of energy until lunchtime, and you will be less likely to buy biscuits or crisps during the morning.

It is also a good idea to (4) ______ attention to how much sugar there is in the food you buy. Many products which are (5) ______ as healthy, such as fruit yoghurts and cereal bars, actually contain a surprising amount of it. Reading the labels carefully in the supermarket only takes a few minutes.

Finally, try not to eat your meals in front of the television or your phone. When your mind is on something else, it is easy to eat far more than you need without (6) ______ it.

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (1).
questions.explanation: The fixed collocation is 'make changes' ('the secret is to make small changes'). We do not say 'do changes', 'take changes' or 'get changes' in English.
options: a) get
b) do
c) take
d) make

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (2).
questions.explanation: To 'skip breakfast' means not to eat it, which matches 'because you are in a hurry'. 'Passing', 'dropping' and 'jumping' are not used with a meal to mean not eating it.
options: a) skipping
b) passing
c) dropping
d) jumping

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (3).
questions.explanation: The pattern is 'keep somebody + adjective': porridge 'will keep you full of energy'. 'Stay' and 'remain' cannot take an object ('you'), and 'hold you full of energy' is not possible.
options: a) remain
b) keep
c) stay
d) hold

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (4).
questions.explanation: The fixed expression is 'pay attention to' something: 'pay attention to how much sugar there is'. 'Make', 'put' and 'take' do not go with 'attention' in this way.
options: a) make
b) pay
c) put
d) take

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (5).
questions.explanation: Products are 'advertised as healthy' when companies sell them with this message, which contrasts with 'actually contain a surprising amount' of sugar. We cannot say a product is 'informed', 'announced' or 'noticed as healthy'.
options: a) advertised
b) informed
c) announced
d) noticed

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (6).
questions.explanation: 'Without noticing it' means without realising what is happening: when your mind is on something else, you eat too much and don't notice. 'Looking it' and 'caring it' are not grammatical (we say 'look at' and 'care about'), and 'paying it' makes no sense here.
options: a) caring
b) paying
c) noticing
d) looking

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 6.
lesenParts.text:
Last Saturday, more than eighty volunteers took part (1) ______ our town's first beach clean-up day at Sandy Bay. The idea came from a group of students at the local college, who had become worried about the amount of rubbish on the shore.

Everyone got gloves and a bag and was given one section of the beach to clean, from the car park to the rocks at the far end. You wouldn't expect to find a fridge on a beach, (2) ______ you? Well, we found two! Most of the rubbish, however, was plastic. We counted how (3) ______ bottles we collected: over six hundred. By lunchtime there was (4) ______ much rubbish for one lorry, and the council had to send a second one.

'I found (5) ______ hard to believe how dirty the beach was,' said Jess Taylor, one of the organisers. 'But people who had never met were chatting and laughing together all day.'

The students now hope to hold a clean-up every spring, (6) ______ or not the council helps them again.

questions.question: Gap (1): More than eighty volunteers took part ____ our town's first beach clean-up day.
questions.explanation: 'Take part in something' is a fixed expression meaning 'join an activity'. 'Part' is always followed by 'in' before the event.

questions.question: Gap (2): You wouldn't expect to find a fridge on a beach, ____ you?
questions.explanation: This is a question tag. The main sentence uses 'wouldn't', so the positive tag repeats the same modal: 'would you?'. 'Do you' or 'will you' do not match 'wouldn't'.

questions.question: Gap (3): We counted how ____ bottles we collected: over six hundred.
questions.explanation: 'Bottles' is a plural countable noun, so we ask about quantity with 'how many'. 'How much' is used with uncountable nouns, and 'how few' does not fit 'over six hundred'.

questions.question: Gap (4): The council had to send a second one to take it all ____.
questions.explanation: 'Too much ... for' means more than something can hold: the rubbish did not fit in one lorry, so the council had to send a second one.

questions.question: Gap (5): I found ____ hard to believe how dirty the beach was.
questions.explanation: In 'find + it + adjective + to-infinitive', 'it' is an empty object that stands for the idea that follows ('to believe how dirty the beach was'). Without 'it' the sentence is not correct.

questions.question: Gap (6): The students now hope to hold a clean-up every spring, ____ or not the council helps them again.
questions.explanation: 'Whether or not' means 'it does not matter if'. The students will do it in any case. 'If' is not possible directly before 'or not'.

Woman: Have you found your phone yet?
Man: Yes, finally. I was sure I'd left it at the gym, so I rang them, but nobody had handed it in.
Woman: Did you look in the kitchen? That's where you usually put it.
Man: I did, twice. In the end it was under the passenger seat in the car. It must have fallen out of my pocket when I drove home.

Dad: What are you having, Ben? The pizza looks good.
Ben: I had pizza last night at Leo's house. I was going to have a salad, but it says here it comes with fish, and I don't like fish.
Dad: The pasta with tomato sauce, then?
Ben: Yes, that's what I'll have.

Man: Are you still going swimming on Tuesdays, Amy?
Amy: No, I gave that up last month. The pool's too far away. I've joined the tennis club near school instead. I've only had two lessons so far, but I love it.
Man: Your brother plays basketball, doesn't he?
Amy: Yes, but that's not for me. I'm too short!

Mum: Have you decided what to get Josh for his birthday?
Girl: Well, I was going to get him a book about football, but he's got loads of those already.
Mum: What about a new football shirt?
Girl: Dad's already bought him one. So I've gone for that new board game he keeps talking about, the one with the space cards. I'll pick it up from the shop on Saturday.

Man: Hi Sara, it's Tom. About the film tonight. The website said it starts at quarter to seven, but I've just phoned the cinema and they've changed it. It's half past seven now, because of some technical problem. So let's still meet at quarter past six for something to eat first. Then we'll have plenty of time. See you later!

Woman: Hello, this is Karen from the community centre, calling about the yoga class on Thursday. You won't need trainers, because we do everything in bare feet. We provide the mats, but please bring your own towel, as we don't have enough for everyone. And don't worry about a notebook. I'll email you the exercises afterwards.

Woman: My bike's got a flat tyre, so I can't cycle in tomorrow.
Man: Will you get the bus, then?
Woman: I thought about it, but there are roadworks on the main road and the buses are taking ages. It's only forty minutes if I walk, and the weather's supposed to be lovely, so I'll just do that.

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 2.

Woman: If we drive to Edinburgh, we can stop wherever we like on the way.
Man: True, but it's eight hours at the wheel, and parking in the city centre is a nightmare.
Woman: Mm, fair point. And on the train we could read or sleep.
Man: Exactly. And it's not much more expensive if we book now.
Woman: Right, let's do that. But I'm not getting up at five to catch the first one!
Man: No, the one at ten is fine. What about the hotel?
Woman: I'd still prefer somewhere outside the centre. It's quieter.
Man: Hmm. We can sort that out later.

Man: So how was the camping trip? You weren't very keen before you went.
Woman: I know! I thought I'd hate sleeping in a tent, and when it rained on the first night I nearly came home. But honestly, it turned out to be one of the best holidays I've ever had. The campsite was lovely, it cost almost nothing, and I didn't miss my phone at all.
Man: So you'd go again?
Woman: Definitely.

Man: Good morning, Skyway Airlines. Is this about the delays on today's flights?
Woman: No, no, my flight isn't until next week. I'm booked to Rome on the fourteenth, reference AB172. My sister's wedding has been moved, so I won't need to be there until the sixteenth. Could you put me on a flight that day instead? I'm happy to pay the difference. Oh, and I've already read the information about hand luggage, so I don't need to ask about that.
Man: Let me see what I can do.

Man: You're off to Spain again? Visiting your cousins?
Woman: Not this time. They're coming over here in the summer. I've booked a two-week course in Seville. My Spanish is getting really rusty, and I'll need it for my new job.
Man: Lucky you. Seville's near the coast, isn't it?
Woman: Not that near, and anyway I doubt I'll have time for the beach. There are classes every morning and homework every evening!

Woman: How was the hotel in Lisbon?
Man: The rooms were a bit small, and I'd read online that the street outside was noisy, but actually we didn't hear a thing at night. What I really liked was that it was right in the old town, so we could walk everywhere. The breakfast was great too, lots of fresh fruit and local cakes.
Woman: Sounds perfect.

Woman: I'm thinking of doing a weekend in Paris. Have you ever done a city break?
Man: A couple. They're not as expensive as people think, if you book early. And I don't mind all the walking, actually. My problem is that by the time you've found your way around, it's time to go home. I'd rather go somewhere for a whole week and really get to know the place.

horenParts.transcript:
Mrs Hughes: Good afternoon, everyone. I'm Mrs Hughes, and I'm going to give you the main details of next term's school trip to Barcelona. We'll be away for five days, from the second to the sixth of April. We'll be flying from Manchester, not Liverpool as I said in my first letter, so please remember that.

In Barcelona we'll be staying in a youth hostel near the beach. Students will share rooms of four, and each room has its own bathroom. Breakfast and dinner are included, but you'll have to buy your own lunch, so bring some extra money for that.

On the first full day we'll visit the famous church, the Sagrada Família, and in the afternoon there's a guided walk around the old part of the city. On the Thursday we're going to spend the morning at a local secondary school, where you'll have lessons with Spanish students of your own age. Several of you asked about the football stadium. Unfortunately, it's closed for building work while we're there, so instead we'll go to the science museum, which I promise is great fun.

The total cost of the trip is three hundred and ninety pounds. You need to pay a deposit of eighty pounds by the end of this month, and the rest before the fifteenth of February.

As for what to pack, the weather in April can be quite changeable, so bring a waterproof jacket as well as sun cream. And please don't forget your passport. Every year somebody leaves it at home! Mobile phones are allowed, but you must hand them in to a teacher at ten o'clock each night.

If you have any questions, please email me rather than phoning the school office. Thank you.

horenParts.transcript:
Interviewer: My guest today is Hannah Price, who at just twenty-four is head chef at her own restaurant. Hannah, how did it all start?
Hannah: I was sixteen and I got a Saturday job washing up in a hotel kitchen. I'd always loved cooking at home, so I thought I knew what to expect, but I was shocked. The heat, the noise, twelve hours on your feet… I honestly wasn't sure I'd last. Funnily enough, I didn't mind the washing-up itself. It was nice just to be able to watch the chefs.
Interviewer: And then you went to catering college.
Hannah: That's right. People assume college taught me to cook, but honestly I learnt most of my skills in real kitchens. The written work was easy for me, actually, because I've always liked reading about food. What really mattered was that my tutors knew everyone in the business. One of them introduced me to the chef who gave me my first proper job.
Interviewer: Lots of young people get interested in cooking through TV competitions. What do you think of them?
Hannah: My mum loves them, and she's always telling me to apply for one, but I'd never do it, and I don't really watch them myself. My problem is that they make it look as if being a chef is all about exciting moments and big prizes. Real restaurant work is mostly cooking the same dishes perfectly, night after night.
Interviewer: Two years ago you opened your own restaurant. Why?
Hannah: Everyone thinks it's about the money, but I earn less now than when I worked for someone else! And my last boss was brilliant. I still ring him for advice. The real reason was that I wanted to cook with ingredients from the farms around here, where I grew up. It's the kind of food nobody in the city was serving.
Interviewer: What's it like being such a young head chef?
Hannah: Inside my kitchen, it's fine. My team know what I can do. But suppliers sometimes ask to speak to 'the chef' when I'm standing right in front of them, and that still annoys me. I don't think being young makes me better or worse at cooking, and I've spent eight years in kitchens, so experience isn't really the issue.
Interviewer: Finally, what would you say to young people who want to become chefs?
Hannah: Don't sign up for a course straight away. Get a part-time job in a real kitchen first, even if it's just washing up, and see if you can cope with it. Plenty of people discover it isn't for them, and that's fine. And don't try to learn every kind of food. Getting a few dishes really right is worth much more.

c) She did not get on with her last boss very well.

options: a) Worried that she does not have enough experience.
b) Annoyed that some people don't see her as the chef.
c) Sure that her age makes her a better cook.

questions.explanation: She says 'Get a part-time job in a real kitchen first … and see if you can cope with it'. She tells them not to sign up for a course straight away, and not to try to learn every kind of food.
options: a) Go to catering college as soon as possible.
b) Get some experience in a real kitchen first.
c) Learn to cook as many kinds of food as possible.

schreibenParts.task:
You must answer this question. Write your answer in about 100 words.

Read this email from your English-speaking friend, Alex, and the notes you have made.

From: Alex
Subject: Guess what!

Hi!

I've got some great news: I've found a flat to rent, and it's in your neighbourhood! I'm moving in at the end of next month. (Note 1: Great!)

I don't know the area at all yet. What's the best thing about living there? (Note 2: Tell Alex)

I'll need to do a lot of shopping for the flat. Where do you think I should go? (Note 3: Suggest…)

And would you like to help me on moving day? I'll buy you lunch! (Note 4: Yes, but…)

See you soon,
Alex

Write your email to Alex using all the notes.

Choose ONE of these questions. Write your answer in about 100 words.

Question A: Article
You see this notice on an English-language website for teenagers.

Articles wanted!
My ideal home
Where would your ideal home be? What would it look like, and what would you have in it? Why would it be perfect for you?
The best articles will be published on our website.

Write your article.

Your English teacher has asked you to write a story.
Your story must begin with this sentence:
The old house at the end of the street was finally sold.

Write your story.

sprechenParts.title: Part 1 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
Answer the examiner's questions about yourself. Give full answers, with reasons or examples.

1. What's your name? Where do you live?
2. What do you usually have for breakfast?
3. Who does most of the cooking in your home?
4. What's your favourite meal of the day? Why?
5. Tell us about a meal you really enjoyed recently.
6. Do you prefer eating at home or eating out? Why?

sprechenParts.title: Part 2 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation: Look at the photograph. It shows a family sharing a meal together at home. Tell us what you can see in the photograph. Talk about the people, the food, the place and what you think is happening. You have about one minute.

sprechenParts.title: Part 3 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
Talk together with your partner. Your class wants to have a meal together to celebrate the end of the school year. Here are some ideas for the meal:

a barbecue in the park
a meal at a pizza restaurant
everyone cooks a dish at home and brings it to school
a picnic on the beach
cooking a meal together in the school kitchen

Talk together about the different ideas and say which would be most enjoyable for the class. Then decide which idea is best.

sprechenParts.title: Part 4 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
Discuss these questions with your partner and the examiner:

1. Do you enjoy cooking? What can you cook?
2. Do you think young people should learn to cook at school? Why or why not?
3. What kinds of restaurants are popular in your town?
4. Is it better to eat with your family or with friends? Why?
5. Do people eat more fast food now than in the past? Why do you think this is?

items.signText:
EARLY DEPARTURES
Breakfast in the restaurant starts at 7.00. If you are leaving before then, please order a packed breakfast at reception before 10 pm the night before. You can collect it from reception from 5.30 a.m.
items.question: What should guests do if they need breakfast before 7.00?
options: a) Go to reception at 10 p.m. to have something to eat.
b) Collect a packed breakfast from the restaurant at 5.30.
c) Ask at reception for a packed breakfast the evening before.
items.explanation: The notice says 'please order a packed breakfast at reception before 10 pm the night before'. The breakfast is collected from reception, not from the restaurant, and 10 pm is the latest time to order, not a time to eat.

items.signText:
Dear Mr Price,
Thank you for your booking. Unfortunately, the sea-view room you asked for is not available on your first night. We can give you a room at the back that night and move you into a sea-view room the next day, at no extra cost. Please let us know if this is acceptable.
Harbour Hotel
items.question: Why has the hotel written to Mr Price?
options: a) To ask him to agree to a change for one night.
b) To offer him a cheaper room for his whole stay.
c) To tell him that his booking has been cancelled.
items.explanation: The sea-view room is 'not available on your first night', so the hotel offers another room that night and asks him to 'let us know if this is acceptable'. The change is only for the first night, the price stays the same ('at no extra cost'), and the booking is not cancelled.

items.signText: Sam – the tourist office has no tickets left for Saturday's boat trip. There are still a few for Sunday at 10, but it finishes at 1, which is after our train leaves. Do you want me to book them and change the train, or shall we forget the trip? Let me know by 5. Mia
items.question: What does Mia want Sam to do?
options: a) Tell her whether she should book the Sunday trip.
b) Go to the tourist office before 5 o'clock.
c) Change their train tickets to a later time on Sunday.
items.explanation: Mia asks 'Do you want me to book them and change the train, or shall we forget the trip? Let me know by 5.' She wants Sam's decision. She offers to change the train herself, so Sam does not have to do it, and nobody needs to go to the office by 5 – that is only when she needs an answer.

items.signText:
FREE CITY WALKING TOURS
Tours leave from outside this office every day at 10.30 and 14.30. There is no need to book – just turn up. Our guides are always grateful for tips. Groups of more than ten people, please contact us in advance.
items.question: What does the notice say about the walking tours?
options: a) Visitors have to pay the guide at the end.
b) Large groups should arrange their tour beforehand.
c) Everyone must book a place at the office the day before.
items.explanation: 'Groups of more than ten people, please contact us in advance' means big groups should arrange it beforehand. The notice says 'There is no need to book – just turn up', and the tours are free: tips are welcome but not required.

items.signText:
SWIMMING POOL
Open daily 7.00–21.00.
Children under 12 must be with an adult at all times.
The pool will be closed on Thursday morning for cleaning, but the gym will stay open as usual.
items.question: What does the sign say?
options: a) Children are not allowed in the pool on Thursday.
b) The gym is closed on Thursday morning.
c) Young children cannot swim without an adult.
items.explanation: The sign says 'Children under 12 must be with an adult at all times.' On Thursday morning the pool is closed for everyone, not only children, and it is open again later; the gym 'will stay open as usual'.

lesenParts.text:
Wildlife photographer Emma Hartley talks about her work.

People often imagine that my job involves travelling to beautiful places and taking amazing pictures every day. The truth is rather different. I spend most of my time waiting – sometimes for days – and on many trips I come home without a single photo I'm happy with.

I became interested in wildlife when I was about ten. My grandfather lent me his old camera, and I used to sit in his garden trying to photograph the birds at the feeder. Most of the pictures were terrible, but I loved the challenge of staying still and quiet for so long. I didn't think of photography as a career, though. At university I studied biology, and I planned to become a scientist.

Everything changed during my final year, when I joined a research trip to Scotland to count sea birds. I took my camera along just for fun, but one of the scientists saw my photos and sent them to a nature magazine. To my surprise, they printed three of them. That was when I realised that I could combine my two interests.

The first few years weren't easy. I earned very little and had to work in a camera shop at weekends to pay the rent. But the job taught me a lot about equipment, and I met photographers who gave me useful advice.

Nowadays I work mainly for magazines and conservation organisations. Before a trip, I spend weeks reading about the animal I want to photograph: where it feeds, when it is most active and how it reacts to people. Good preparation matters far more than an expensive camera. Last spring, for example, I wanted to photograph otters in Norway. Local fishermen told me the otters came out at dawn, so I was in my hiding place by four o'clock every morning. On the sixth day, a mother and two young otters appeared just metres away.

The part of the job I find hardest is not the cold or the early mornings but being away from my family. My son is seven now, and I try not to accept jobs that last more than two weeks.

Young people often ask me how to start. My answer is always the same: begin close to home. You don't need to travel to Africa. A local park is full of wildlife if you are patient enough to look for it. And remember that the animal always comes first. If it seems stressed, put your camera down and walk away. No photo is worth frightening an animal.

questions.question: What does Emma say about her job in the first paragraph?
questions.explanation: Emma says 'I spend most of my time waiting – sometimes for days'. She says 'the truth is rather different' from what people imagine, so it is not as exciting as people think, and 'on many trips I come home without a single photo I'm happy with', so good photos are not easy to get.
options: a) It is as exciting as most people think.
b) It is easy to get good photos on most trips.
c) She usually knows exactly when the animals will appear.
d) Most of her time is spent waiting.

questions.question: What did Emma enjoy about photographing birds as a child?
questions.explanation: She says 'I loved the challenge of staying still and quiet for so long'. Her photos were not good ('Most of the pictures were terrible'), and the text does not mention showing them to her grandfather or learning bird names.
options: a) Seeing how good her photos were.
b) Learning the names of different garden birds.
c) Having to be patient and silent for a long time.
d) Showing her pictures to her grandfather in his garden.

questions.question: How did Emma's career as a photographer begin?
questions.explanation: On the research trip 'one of the scientists saw my photos and sent them to a nature magazine', which printed three of them. She went to Scotland 'to count sea birds', not to work for a magazine, and she took her camera 'just for fun'.
options: a) A scientist sent some of her photos to a magazine.
b) She went to Scotland to take photos for a magazine.
c) Her university teachers told her to study photography.
d) A magazine offered her a job when she finished university.

questions.question: What does Emma think about preparing for a trip?
questions.explanation: She reads about where the animal feeds and when it is active, and says 'Good preparation matters far more than an expensive camera.' The fishermen in Norway are only one example, and seeing the otters 'on the sixth day' does not mean she limits her trips to six days.
options: a) Knowing about the animal is more important than having good equipment.
b) She must ask local fishermen for advice before every trip.
c) She needs to buy a more expensive camera for each new animal.
d) She should never plan to stay in one place for more than six days.

questions.question: What advice would Emma give to a young person who wants to photograph wildlife?
questions.explanation: Emma tells young people to 'begin close to home' because 'a local park is full of wildlife', and says 'If it seems stressed, put your camera down and walk away. No photo is worth frightening an animal.' She says 'You don't need to travel to Africa', and earlier that an expensive camera matters less than preparation.
options: a) "Buy the best camera you can afford before you start."
b) "Practise near where you live, and never upset the animals."
c) "Get as close as you can to an animal, even if it seems nervous."
d) "Save up so that you can travel to places like Africa."

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 4.
lesenParts.text:
Most parents have had the same experience. They knock on their teenager's bedroom door at nine o'clock on a Saturday morning. There is no answer. It is easy to think that teenagers are simply lazy. (1) ______

During the teenage years, the body's internal 'clock' changes. This clock controls our daily pattern of sleeping and waking. The brain starts producing melatonin, the chemical that makes us feel sleepy, around two hours later than it did in childhood. (2) ______ But school still starts at the same time, so the alarm goes off long before their bodies are ready to wake up.

Sleep matters at every age, but it is especially important for teenagers. Experts say teenagers need between eight and ten hours of sleep a night. Surveys show that most of them get fewer than seven. (3) ______ Students who sleep too little find it harder to concentrate in class and to remember what they have learnt. They are also more likely to feel anxious or low. They catch colds more often, too. Their results in sport can suffer as well.

Phones make the problem worse. Many teenagers take them to bed and message friends or watch videos until late. (4) ______ The light from the screen also tells the brain that it is still daytime, so melatonin arrives even later.

So what can teenagers do? There are some simple answers. Sleep experts suggest going to bed at the same time every night, even at weekends, and leaving phones in another room. (5) ______ Some schools in the UK and the USA have even started lessons an hour later, and teachers there say that students are more awake and get better marks. Perhaps other schools will soon follow their example.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (1)?
questions.explanation: The sentence before says 'It is easy to think that teenagers are simply lazy.' 'However' contrasts with this idea, and 'a much better explanation' introduces the next paragraph, which explains the body clock. The sentence about online time cannot go here because phones have not been mentioned yet.
options: A) In other words, their bodies are simply not ready for sleep until much later in the evening.
B) It is not just the time they spend online that matters, however.
C) Their teachers, however, did not notice any difference at all.
D) However, scientists now believe that there is a much better explanation.
E) Because of this, teenagers today sleep much longer than their grandparents did.
F) Getting outside in the morning light can help too, because it resets the body clock.
G) The difference may not sound very big, but it can have a serious effect.
H) Sadly, none of the schools that tried this saw any improvement.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (2)?
questions.explanation: 'In other words' repeats the idea that melatonin arrives 'two hours later' in simpler words. The next sentence, 'But school still starts at the same time', contrasts with 'not ready for sleep until much later', and 'their bodies' is repeated in 'before their bodies are ready to wake up'. The sentence saying teenagers 'sleep much longer' contradicts the article.
options: A) In other words, their bodies are simply not ready for sleep until much later in the evening.
B) It is not just the time they spend online that matters, however.
C) Their teachers, however, did not notice any difference at all.
D) However, scientists now believe that there is a much better explanation.
E) Because of this, teenagers today sleep much longer than their grandparents did.
F) Getting outside in the morning light can help too, because it resets the body clock.
G) The difference may not sound very big, but it can have a serious effect.
H) Sadly, none of the schools that tried this saw any improvement.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (3)?
questions.explanation: 'The difference' refers to 'between eight and ten hours' needed and 'fewer than seven' actually slept. 'A serious effect' is then explained by the list that follows: students find it harder to concentrate, feel anxious and catch colds. The sentence saying teachers 'did not notice any difference' contradicts these effects.
options: A) In other words, their bodies are simply not ready for sleep until much later in the evening.
B) It is not just the time they spend online that matters, however.
C) Their teachers, however, did not notice any difference at all.
D) However, scientists now believe that there is a much better explanation.
E) Because of this, teenagers today sleep much longer than their grandparents did.
F) Getting outside in the morning light can help too, because it resets the body clock.
G) The difference may not sound very big, but it can have a serious effect.
H) Sadly, none of the schools that tried this saw any improvement.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (4)?
questions.explanation: The sentence before describes teenagers who 'message friends or watch videos until late' – the time they spend online. The gap sentence says this is not the only problem, and the next sentence gives the second problem with 'also': 'The light from the screen also tells the brain that it is still daytime.' The sentence about morning light cannot go here because 'help too' needs an earlier piece of advice.
options: A) In other words, their bodies are simply not ready for sleep until much later in the evening.
B) It is not just the time they spend online that matters, however.
C) Their teachers, however, did not notice any difference at all.
D) However, scientists now believe that there is a much better explanation.
E) Because of this, teenagers today sleep much longer than their grandparents did.
F) Getting outside in the morning light can help too, because it resets the body clock.
G) The difference may not sound very big, but it can have a serious effect.
H) Sadly, none of the schools that tried this saw any improvement.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (5)?
questions.explanation: The sentence before gives two pieces of advice from sleep experts, and 'can help too' adds a third. The next sentence, 'Some schools ... have even started lessons an hour later', adds one more solution. The sentence saying 'none of the schools that tried this saw any improvement' cannot go here: it refers to 'this' before the later start has been mentioned, and it contradicts the teachers, who say students 'get better marks'.
options: A) In other words, their bodies are simply not ready for sleep until much later in the evening.
B) It is not just the time they spend online that matters, however.
C) Their teachers, however, did not notice any difference at all.
D) However, scientists now believe that there is a much better explanation.
E) Because of this, teenagers today sleep much longer than their grandparents did.
F) Getting outside in the morning light can help too, because it resets the body clock.
G) The difference may not sound very big, but it can have a serious effect.
H) Sadly, none of the schools that tried this saw any improvement.

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 5.
lesenParts.text:
Last April I ran my first marathon through the streets of my home city. I had (1) ______ up running two years earlier because I wanted to get fit, but at the beginning I couldn't run for more than ten minutes (2) ______ stopping. It was a friend from work who finally (3) ______ me to enter the race.

I found a training plan online and (4) ______ my distance a little every week. I trained three times a week, in the rain, in the dark and sometimes even in the snow. By the end, some of my long runs were taking more than three hours.

On the day of the race, the (5) ______ was amazing. Thousands of people stood along the streets, clapping and shouting our names, and bands were playing music on almost every corner. By kilometre 35 my legs were really hurting and I wanted to stop, but the crowd kept me going.

I crossed the finish line in four hours and ten minutes. I was completely exhausted, but I have never felt so (6) ______ of myself. I've already signed up for next year's race.

questions.question: Gap (1): I had ____ up running two years earlier because I wanted to get fit.
questions.explanation: 'Take up' means to start a new hobby or activity: 'I had taken up running'. 'Get up' means to leave your bed, 'put up' means to build or raise something, and 'make up' means to invent – none of them mean starting a sport.
options: a) got
b) put
c) taken
d) made

questions.question: Gap (2): I couldn't run for more than ten minutes ____ stopping.
questions.explanation: 'Without stopping' means continuously, with no break. 'Unless' must be followed by a clause (unless I stopped), 'instead' needs 'of' (instead of stopping), and 'except stopping' does not make sense here.
options: a) instead
b) without
c) except
d) unless

questions.question: Gap (3): It was a friend from work who finally ____ me to enter the race.
questions.explanation: Only 'persuade' is followed by object + to-infinitive: 'persuaded me to enter'. We say 'suggested that I enter', and 'made' and 'let' are followed by the infinitive without 'to' (made me enter, let me enter).
options: a) persuaded
b) suggested
c) made
d) let

questions.question: Gap (4): I found a training plan online and ____ my distance a little every week.
questions.explanation: 'Increase' takes an object and means to make something bigger: 'increased my distance'. 'Grow' and 'rise' do not take an object here (my distance rose), and 'add' needs 'to' (added to my distance).
options: a) grew
b) rose
c) added
d) increased

questions.question: Gap (5): On the day of the race, the ____ was amazing.
questions.explanation: 'Atmosphere' is the feeling created by the people in a place, and the next sentence describes it: people 'clapping and shouting our names' and bands playing. 'Climate' is the usual weather of a region over many years, 'surface' is the top of the road, and 'nature' means plants and animals – none of these are described.
options: a) atmosphere
b) climate
c) surface
d) nature

questions.question: Gap (6): I was completely exhausted, but I have never felt so ____ of myself.
questions.explanation: The fixed phrase is 'proud of yourself'. 'Pleased' and 'happy' are followed by 'with' (pleased with myself), and 'glad' is not used with 'of myself'.
options: a) glad
b) proud
c) pleased
d) happy

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 6.
lesenParts.text:
When I was a child, I always wanted to learn the guitar, but my parents couldn't afford lessons. Two years ago, on my fortieth birthday, I finally bought one and tried to teach (1) ______ by watching videos online.

The beginning was hard. My fingers hurt quite (2) ______ lot, and they weren't strong (3) ______ to press the strings down properly. After a month I nearly gave (4) ______ playing.

Then my daughter found me a teacher, Sara, and everything changed. She explained that the pain happens to all beginners and that the skin gets harder with practice. Apart (5) ______ the technique, she has taught me to read music and to play in a band with other adult learners, which is the best part of my week.

I now try to practise for twenty minutes every evening (6) ______ I am working late. Next month our music school is having a concert, and I am going to play in front of an audience for the first time. I'm nervous, but also very excited.

questions.question: Gap (1): I finally bought one and tried to teach ____ by watching videos online.
questions.explanation: The subject 'I' is also the person who learns, so the verb 'teach' needs the reflexive pronoun 'myself' ('teach myself' = learn without a teacher). 'Me' is not correct when the object is the same person as the subject.

questions.question: Gap (2): My fingers hurt quite ____ lot.
questions.explanation: 'Quite a lot' is a fixed expression meaning 'very much'. 'Lot' needs the article 'a' here; 'quite the lot' or 'quite lot' are not correct.

questions.question: Gap (3): They weren't strong ____ to press the strings down properly.
questions.explanation: 'Adjective + enough + to-infinitive' says whether something has the necessary quality: the fingers did not have the strength needed. 'Enough' comes after the adjective ('strong enough'); 'too' and 'very' go before it.

questions.question: Gap (4): After a month I nearly gave ____ playing.
questions.explanation: 'Give up + -ing' is a phrasal verb meaning 'stop doing something'. The writer found it hard and almost stopped. 'Gave in' is not followed by an -ing form, and 'gave away' needs an object like 'the guitar'.

questions.question: Gap (5): Apart ____ the technique, she has taught me to read music and to play in a band.
questions.explanation: 'Apart from' means 'as well as / in addition to'. 'Apart' is always followed by 'from' in this expression.

questions.question: Gap (6): I now try to practise for twenty minutes every evening ____ I am working late.
questions.explanation: 'Unless' means 'except if': the writer practises every evening, but not on the evenings when they work late. 'If' or 'when' would mean the opposite (practising only on those late evenings).

horenParts.transcript:
Man: Excuse me, I'm here for the Year 10 parents' evening. Is it in the library, like last term?
Woman: Not this time, I'm afraid. The library's being painted this week. We'd planned to use the dining room, but it's too small for all the teachers' tables, so everyone's in the main hall. Just go down this corridor and it's the double doors on your left.
Man: Great, thanks very much.

Girl: Dad, Mrs Palmer says everyone in the orchestra has to take something to the concert tomorrow evening.
Man: Not your music stand again? It's still in the car from last time.
Girl: No, the school's got plenty of those now. And they've borrowed chairs from the church hall, so we don't need to bring our own. It's the lights, actually. The hall will be quite dark while we're playing, so we all need a small torch to read our music.
Man: I think there's one in the kitchen drawer. I'll check the batteries.

Girl: Are you going to be in the talent show, Josh? I thought you might play your guitar.
Boy: I did think about it, but loads of people are doing music. And I'm definitely not dancing. You've seen me try!
Girl: So what are you going to do, then?
Boy: I've been writing some funny stories about school life. I'm going to stand up on stage and tell jokes. Mr Grant says it's fine as long as I'm kind about the teachers.
Girl: That'll be brilliant.

Girl: Guess what, Gran? I came first in the school art competition!
Woman: Oh, well done, love! What did you get? Last year the winner got a big box of paints, didn't they?
Girl: They did, but I've already got loads of paints. This year the winner got a ticket for the new exhibition at the city gallery, and I can take someone with me. The girl who came second got a book of famous paintings.
Woman: That sounds lovely. So who are you taking?
Girl: You, of course!

Boy: Did you hear about the Year 9 trip? We were supposed to be going to the castle, but Mr Hughes says the coach company can't do that date.
Girl: So is it cancelled?
Boy: No, they've changed it. We're going to the science museum in the city instead, because the train goes straight there. Some people wanted the farm park, but that's closed until the spring.
Girl: Oh well, the museum's got that new space exhibition, so I don't mind.

Woman: Hello, this is a message for all parents from Kingsmead School. Sports day is going ahead this Friday, but please note that the start time has changed. The races were going to begin at half past ten, but because very hot weather is forecast for the afternoon, the first races will now start at quarter past nine. Students should arrive at school at nine o'clock as usual, wearing their PE kit, and bring a bottle of water. Thank you.

Woman: You're not playing computer games already, are you? What about your homework?
Boy: I've done the maths worksheet. I finished it at lunchtime. And the science poster isn't due until next Friday.
Woman: So there's nothing else?
Boy: Well, there's the history essay. Mr Dean wants it on his desk first thing tomorrow morning, and I've only written the introduction.
Woman: Then the games can wait, can't they?

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 2.
horenParts.transcript:
Woman: So you've started your engineering course. What's it like?
Man: It's hard work. The lectures are long, but the lecturers make them really interesting. What I love most, though, is the time in the workshop. Last week we built a small bridge and tested how much weight it could take. That's why I chose engineering, really.
Woman: And it's four years, isn't it? That seems a long time.
Man: It goes quickly when you enjoy it.

Girl: I heard you're giving up your job at the café. Is it the money?
Boy: No, the pay's actually quite good for a weekend job, and Sue, the manager, is lovely. It's just that my exams start in May, and at the moment I'm working every Saturday and Sunday. I've got so much revision to do that something has to go.
Girl: Will they let you come back in the summer?
Boy: Sue says they will, so that's good.

Man: So, what do you think of the new office, now we've been here a week?
Woman: I was worried it'd be really noisy with everyone in one big room, but actually it's been fine. And because the design team sit right next to us now, I can just turn round and ask them things instead of sending emails. We've sorted out more problems this week than in the whole of last month.
Man: The journey's worse for me, though. It's a much longer walk from the station.
Woman: Oh, it's about the same for me.

Woman: Have you got a minute, Mr Clarke?
Man: Of course, Helen. If it's about your holiday dates, I've already said yes.
Woman: Thanks, but it's not that. I heard that Tom's team is behind with the new website. I've finished all my own work for this month, so I wondered if I could join them for a couple of weeks.
Man: That would be a big help, actually. Tom will be delighted.

Boy: How was the interview for the summer job at the museum?
Girl: They kept me waiting for twenty minutes, which wasn't ideal, but I didn't really mind because it gave me time to calm down. And then it went better than I expected. I'd read all about the museum beforehand, so I could answer all their questions, and they even laughed at my joke about the dinosaurs!
Boy: It sounds like you'll get it.
Girl: Well, I really think I've got a good chance.

Woman: How's your online Spanish course going?
Man: Well, I'm not sure about the teacher. She talks really fast and she doesn't always explain the grammar.
Woman: I've found that with mine too. But for thirty pounds a term, you can't really complain, can you? The evening class at the college costs four times that.
Man: That's true. You get a lot for the price. And the lessons are only forty minutes, which suits me.
Woman: Me too. I couldn't concentrate for any longer after work.

Boy: Sue says they will, so that's good.

questions.question: You will hear two students talking about a part-time job. Why is the boy leaving his job at the café?
questions.explanation: The boy says his exams start in May and 'I've got so much revision to do that something has to go'. He says the pay is 'quite good' and the manager 'is lovely', so the other reasons are wrong.
options: a) He isn't paid enough.
b) He doesn't get on with his manager.
c) He needs more time to study.

segments.label: Recording 3
segments.transcript:
Man: So, what do you think of the new office, now we've been here a week?
Woman: I was worried it'd be really noisy with everyone in one big room, but actually it's been fine. And because the design team sit right next to us now, I can just turn round and ask them things instead of sending emails. We've sorted out more problems this week than in the whole of last month.
Man: The journey's worse for me, though. It's a much longer walk from the station.
Woman: Oh, it's about the same for me.

questions.question: You will hear two colleagues talking about their new office. What does the woman think about it?
questions.explanation: The woman says she can 'just turn round and ask' the design team instead of sending emails, and they have 'sorted out more problems'. She expected noise but says 'actually it's been fine', and it is the man, not the woman, who has a longer journey; for her it is 'about the same'.
options: a) It is too noisy with everyone in one big room.
b) It makes it easier to share information.
c) It takes her longer to get there.

segments.label: Recording 4
segments.transcript:
Woman: Have you got a minute, Mr Clarke?
Man: Of course, Helen. If it's about your holiday dates, I've already said yes.
Woman: Thanks, but it's not that. I heard that Tom's team is behind with the new website. I've finished all my own work for this month, so I wondered if I could join them for a couple of weeks.
Man: That would be a big help, actually. Tom will be delighted.

questions.question: You will hear a woman talking to her manager. Why has she come to see him?
questions.explanation: Helen has finished her own work and asks 'if I could join them for a couple of weeks' to help Tom's team with the website. She says 'it's not that' when the manager mentions her holiday, and she mentions that Tom's team is behind only to explain her offer, not to complain.
options: a) To offer to help with some work
b) To ask for some time off
c) To complain about a colleague

segments.label: Recording 5
segments.transcript:
Boy: How was the interview for the summer job at the museum?
Girl: They kept me waiting for twenty minutes, which wasn't ideal, but I didn't really mind because it gave me time to calm down. And then it went better than I expected. I'd read all about the museum beforehand, so I could answer all their questions, and they even laughed at my joke about the dinosaurs!
Boy: It sounds like you'll get it.
Girl: Well, I really think I've got a good chance.

questions.question: You will hear a girl talking about a job interview. How does she feel about it?
questions.explanation: The girl says 'it went better than I expected' and 'I really think I've got a good chance'. She was kept waiting but 'didn't really mind', and she had prepared well: 'I'd read all about the museum beforehand'.
options: a) Worried that she wasn't prepared
b) Pleased with how she did
c) Annoyed that it started late

segments.label: Recording 6
segments.transcript:
Woman: How's your online Spanish course going?
Man: Well, I'm not sure about the teacher. She talks really fast and she doesn't always explain the grammar.
Woman: I've found that with mine too. But for thirty pounds a term, you can't really complain, can you? The evening class at the college costs four times that.
Man: That's true. You get a lot for the price. And the lessons are only forty minutes, which suits me.
Woman: Me too. I couldn't concentrate for any longer after work.

questions.question: You will hear two friends talking about online language courses. What do they agree about?
questions.explanation: The woman says 'for thirty pounds a term, you can't really complain' and the man agrees: 'That's true. You get a lot for the price.' They both like the forty-minute lessons, so they do not think they are too long, and both say their teachers do not always explain things well.
options: a) The courses are good value for money.
b) The lessons are too long to follow after work.
c) The teachers explain things clearly.

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 3.
horenParts.transcript:
Woman: Good morning, everyone. I'm Kate Morris, the manager of the new Riverside Sports Centre, and I'd like to tell you what we're offering when we open next month. The opening day is Saturday the twelfth of March. We were hoping to open in February, but the builders needed a little more time to finish everything.

The centre has a twenty-five-metre swimming pool, a sports hall and a gym. But the thing we're proudest of is our climbing wall, which is the tallest in the region. Beginners are very welcome. You don't need any experience, because an instructor will be with you all the time.

Membership costs thirty-two pounds a month for adults, and students and people over sixty-five pay twenty pounds. And if you join before the opening day, your first month is completely free.

We've also got something special on Sunday mornings. The pool will be open only for parents and children, and there'll be games and floating toys in the water.

Lots of people have asked us about getting here. There is a car park, but it only has forty spaces, so we'd really recommend coming by bike. We've put a large bike shelter right next to the main entrance. The number fourteen bus stops outside too, but it only runs once an hour.

Finally, if you'd like to look around before you join, we're running free tours every afternoon this week. They leave from the reception desk at four o'clock, and they take about half an hour. I hope to see lots of you there.

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 4.
horenParts.transcript:
Interviewer: My guest today is Leila Ahmed, who designs video games. Leila, how did you first get interested in making games?
Leila: People often think I had a teacher who pushed me, but actually my teachers thought games were a complete waste of time. And I certainly didn't expect to get rich! What happened was that as a teenager I used to change the levels in the games I'd bought. I'd add new rooms, make the monsters harder, that kind of thing. I enjoyed that far more than just playing them.
Interviewer: And then you went to university?
Leila: Yes, I studied games design. The programming was hard, and at one point I thought about switching to an art course, but I'm glad I didn't. Looking back, the most useful thing was the group projects. In this industry nobody works alone, and that's where I learnt to listen to other people's ideas and share my own.
Interviewer: What was your first job like?
Leila: It was at a small company in Manchester. I'd imagined I'd spend my days inventing characters, but in fact I spent most of my time playing the same level again and again to find mistakes. I had no idea how much testing goes into a game. It wasn't boring exactly, it taught me to be patient, and my boss was very kind to me. I just hadn't expected it.
Interviewer: What do you think makes a really good game?
Leila: Well, everyone talks about the graphics, and of course a good story helps. But for me, if a player can't understand what to do in the first two minutes, they'll stop playing, however beautiful the game looks. So simple rules come first. Everything else is built on that.
Interviewer: Some parents worry that young people spend too much time on games. What's your view?
Leila: I don't think games are bad for young people at all. Lots of them teach you to solve problems. But I've got two children myself, and they have to go outside and see their friends as well. An hour or so after their homework seems about right to me. And I don't mind whether it's an educational game or not. To be honest, a lot of educational games aren't very good!
Interviewer: Finally, what would you say to listeners who'd like to design games?
Leila: Don't wait. You don't have to go to university first, and you certainly don't need to start as a tester like I did. There are free programs that let you build a small game in a weekend. Make something simple, show it to your friends and listen carefully to what they say. That's how you learn.
Interviewer: Leila Ahmed, thank you very much.

options: a) She felt her boss at the small company treated her unfairly.

schreibenParts.task:
Read this email from your English-speaking friend Sam and the notes you have made.

From: Sam
Subject: Maya's birthday

Hi!

It's Maya's birthday on the 18th and I'd love us to plan something special for her. [Note: Great idea!]

I was thinking of either a picnic in the park or going bowling. Which do you think she'd prefer? [Note: Say which and why]

I'd also like to buy her a present together with you. Have you got any ideas? [Note: Suggest...]

Could we meet this weekend to organise everything? [Note: Yes, tell Sam when]

Speak soon,
Sam

Write your email to Sam using all the notes. Write about 100 words.

Choose ONE of these questions. Write about 100 words.

Article
You see this notice on an English-language website for teenagers.

Articles wanted!
A celebration I will never forget
Tell us about a celebration you will always remember. What were you celebrating? Who was there? Why was it so special?
The best articles will appear on our website.

Write your article.

Story
Your English teacher has asked you to write a story. Your story must begin with this sentence:

Everyone shouted 'Surprise!' when I walked in.

Write your story.

items.signText:
SWIMMING POOL USERS
From 1 June, children under 8 must have an adult with them in the water at all times. Older children may swim on their own but need to show a pool card, which they can get from reception.
items.question: What is the new rule at the swimming pool?
options: a) Children under 8 can get a pool card from reception.
b) Young children may not swim without an adult.
c) All children must swim with an adult at all times.
items.explanation: The notice says 'children under 8 must have an adult with them in the water at all times'. It is not all children, because 'older children may swim on their own', and the pool card is for these older children, not for children under 8.

items.signText: Leo, the tennis courts in the park are fully booked tomorrow, so I've reserved one at the sports centre instead. It's further away, so let's meet at the bus stop at 9.30 rather than 10. Sam
items.question: Why has Sam written to Leo?
options: a) To explain why they need to meet earlier than planned
b) To cancel their game because there are no courts free
c) To ask Leo to book a court at the sports centre
items.explanation: Sam has booked a court at the sports centre, which is 'further away', so Sam suggests meeting 'at 9.30 rather than 10' – earlier than planned. The game is not cancelled, and Sam has already booked the court ('I've reserved one'), so Leo does not need to do it.

items.signText:
YOGA CLASSES
Our Tuesday evening class has become so popular that we have added a second class on Thursdays at the same time. Please book online at least a day before, as places cannot be reserved by phone.
items.question: What is the sports centre telling people?
options: a) The Tuesday yoga class has moved to Thursday.
b) Places in yoga classes can now be booked by phone.
c) There is now an extra yoga class every week.
items.explanation: The centre says 'we have added a second class on Thursdays', so there is one more class each week. The Tuesday class has not moved – the new class is in addition to it – and places 'cannot be reserved by phone'.

items.signText: Dogs are welcome in all areas of the park except the children's playground and the flower garden. Please keep your dog on a lead near the lake between April and July, when birds are nesting.
items.question: What does the sign say about dogs?
options: a) They cannot come into the park between April and July.
b) They must be kept on a lead everywhere in the park.
c) They are not allowed in certain parts of the park.
items.explanation: Dogs are welcome 'in all areas of the park except the children's playground and the flower garden', so there are some parts where they cannot go. Between April and July they can still come in, but must be on a lead only 'near the lake', not everywhere.

items.signText:
PARK CAFÉ
Our kitchen is being repaired this week. Hot meals will not be available until Monday, but you can still buy sandwiches, cold drinks and ice creams at the counter. We are sorry for any inconvenience.
items.question: What does the notice say?
options: a) You can buy cold food this week, but not hot meals.
b) The café is looking for new staff for its kitchen.
c) The café will be completely closed until next Monday.
items.explanation: The notice says 'Hot meals will not be available until Monday, but you can still buy sandwiches, cold drinks and ice creams'. The café is not closed, because the counter is still selling things, and the problem is a repair, not a lack of staff.
