lesenParts.text:
Every Saturday morning, Leah Morgan, 26, takes her guitar and a small speaker to the square outside Bristol's main shopping centre. For the next four hours she sings to anyone who stops to listen. We asked her about life as a street musician.

How did you start?
'Almost by accident. I'd been playing in cafés for a couple of years, but they only paid me in free coffee! One day a friend dared me to play outside the railway station. I was terrified – my hands were shaking so much that I could hardly play the right notes. But a little girl stood in front of me and danced through every song, and by the end I'd completely forgotten my nerves. I went home with more money than I'd ever earned in a café.'

Is it hard work?
'People think we just turn up and play, but there's a lot more to it. In Bristol you need a permit from the city council, and there are rules about how loud you can be and how long you can stay in one place. I also check the weather forecast all the time. Rain is bad, obviously, but a very hot day is almost as bad, because people hurry from shop to shop and don't want to stand still.'

What's the best thing about it?
'The audience is completely honest. In a concert hall, people have paid for a ticket, so they stay even if they're bored. On the street, if you're not good enough, they simply walk away. That can be hard, but it has made me a much better performer. I've learnt to notice straight away when I'm losing people, and to change the song.'

Does anyone ever complain?
'Occasionally. A man who works in one of the shops used to come out and ask me to turn the music down. At first I was annoyed, but then I realised he had to listen to me all day. Now I play my quieter songs when I'm near his door, and he sometimes brings me a cup of tea!'

What are your plans?
'A few people have offered to manage me, and I've recorded some songs, which I sell as downloads. But I'm in no hurry to give up the street. I don't think I'd ever get the same feeling in a studio. Even if I become famous one day – which I doubt – I'd like to come back to the square now and then, just to remind myself where it all began.'

questions.question: What happened the first time Leah played outside the station?
questions.explanation: Leah was terrified at first, but 'a little girl stood in front of me and danced through every song, and by the end I'd completely forgotten my nerves'. She did not stop early, her friend only 'dared' her to play, and she earned 'more money than I'd ever earned in a café', not less.
options: a) Her friend had to help her when she made mistakes.
b) A child's reaction helped her to feel calmer.
c) She earned less money than she usually did in cafés.
d) She felt so nervous that she stopped early.

questions.question: What does Leah say about the weather?
questions.explanation: Leah says 'Rain is bad, obviously, but a very hot day is almost as bad', because people hurry and do not stop. She checks the forecast 'all the time' but never says she refuses to play, and the council rules she mentions are about volume and time, not rain. She does not say that sunny days bring more money; on very hot days people 'don't want to stand still'.
options: a) She never plays when the forecast is bad.
b) People give her more money when it is sunny.
c) The council does not allow street music in the rain.
d) Very hot days can be almost as bad as rain.

questions.question: Why does Leah think playing in the street has made her a better performer?
questions.explanation: Leah says street audiences are honest: 'if you're not good enough, they simply walk away', and 'it has made me a much better performer' because she notices 'when I'm losing people'. She never mentions advice from listeners, and there are rules about 'how loud you can be', so playing louder is not the reason.
options: a) People who stop often give her useful advice.
b) She has to perform for longer than in a concert hall.
c) People leave at once if they don't enjoy it.
d) She has learnt to play much more loudly.

questions.question: How did Leah deal with the complaints from the man in the shop?
questions.explanation: Leah understood that 'he had to listen to me all day', so 'Now I play my quieter songs when I'm near his door'. She still plays in the same square with her speaker, and she does not mention contacting the council about him.
options: a) She stopped using her speaker in the square.
b) She asked the council to speak to the man.
c) She moved to a different part of the square.
d) She changed the songs she played near his shop.

questions.question: What would Leah probably say about her future?
questions.explanation: Leah is 'in no hurry to give up the street', and even if she becomes famous she would 'like to come back to the square now and then'. She says she would not get 'the same feeling in a studio', and she doubts she will become famous ('which I doubt').
options: a) 'Whatever happens, I want to play in the street sometimes.'
b) 'I'm sure that I'll be really famous in a few years' time.'
c) 'As soon as I find a manager, I'll stop playing in the street.'
d) 'I'd much rather record music in a studio than play outside.'

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 4.
lesenParts.text:
Learning a new language as an adult can feel impossible. Three years ago I moved to Lisbon for work without knowing a single word of Portuguese. Today I can chat comfortably with my neighbours and even argue with the plumber. Here is what worked for me.

First, I stopped trying to study for hours at the weekend. (1) ______ Instead, I spent twenty minutes on Portuguese every single day, usually on the bus to work. Short, regular practice turned out to be far more effective than long, tiring sessions.

Second, I learnt the words I actually needed. Textbooks often begin with colours and animals, but I needed to buy bread, pay bills and ask for directions. (2) ______ That list became my first vocabulary book, and because I was using the words every day, I remembered them easily.

My third tip is to accept that you will make mistakes. For months I was so worried about saying something wrong that I hardly spoke at all. (3) ______ She told me that people would be pleased I was trying, and she was right. Most people I met were patient and helpful, and some even corrected me in a friendly way.

It also helps to bring the language into your free time. I changed the language on my phone to Portuguese and started watching films with Portuguese subtitles. (4) ______ After a while, though, I found I could follow a whole film without stopping it once.

Finally, find a reason to speak that has nothing to do with lessons. I joined a local running club, where nobody spoke English. (5) ______ Now some of those runners are my closest friends, and I no longer think about which language I'm speaking.

Learning a language takes time, and there is no magic method. But if you practise a little every day and don't give up, you will be surprised how far you can go.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (1)?
questions.explanation: The writer 'stopped trying to study for hours at the weekend'; the sentence about ending up 'tired and bored' and forgetting everything 'by Monday' gives the reason, and 'Instead, I spent twenty minutes... every single day' follows naturally. The sentence about preferring 'a grammar book on Sunday afternoons' is also about weekend study, but it contradicts the writer's decision to stop.
options: A) Then my landlady, Rosa, noticed how quiet I was and gave me some advice.
B) Of course, my friends back home were sure I would never manage to learn such a difficult language.
C) In the beginning I could only say 'hello' and 'well done', but gradually we started chatting on the long runs.
D) I always ended up tired and bored, and by Monday I had forgotten most of what I had learnt.
E) This is why I still prefer to study with a grammar book on Sunday afternoons.
F) At first this was very frustrating, as I had to pause every few minutes to look up words.
G) So I made a list of every phrase I needed during the week and asked a colleague to translate it.
H) Luckily, everyone there spoke excellent English, so I never felt lost.

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 5.
lesenParts.text:
Twenty years ago, most people were nervous about buying things online. Today, millions of us (1) ______ our weekly shopping without leaving the house. But how do we decide what to buy?

Many shoppers spend a long time reading reviews by other customers before they (2) ______ a decision. A product with hundreds of positive comments is far more likely to sell than one with none, even if it is more expensive.

Price is still important. Lots of people (3) ______ prices on several websites to find the best deal, and some wait for the sales, when shops (4) ______ big discounts.

However, shopping online is not always as easy as it looks. Clothes may not fit, and colours often look different on a screen. That is why many companies now let customers send items back free of (5) ______.

Some experts believe that in the future we will do even more of our shopping online. Others think we will always want to see and touch things first. Whoever is right, one thing is (6) ______: the way we shop has changed for ever.

questions.question: Gap (1): millions of us ____ our weekly shopping without leaving the house.
questions.explanation: The fixed expression is 'do the shopping' / 'do our weekly shopping'. We do not say 'make', 'take' or 'have' our shopping in English.
options: a) do
b) take
c) have
d) make

questions.question: Gap (2): before they ____ a decision.
questions.explanation: The collocation is 'make a decision'. 'Do a decision', 'put a decision' and 'get a decision' are not correct English.
options: a) get
b) make
c) do
d) put

questions.question: Gap (3): Lots of people ____ prices on several websites to find the best deal.
questions.explanation: To find the best deal, people look at the prices on different websites to see which is cheapest: they 'compare prices'. 'Compete' needs 'with' and is about trying to win, 'correct' means remove mistakes, and 'confuse prices' would not help anyone find a good deal.
options: a) correct
b) confuse
c) compete
d) compare

questions.question: Gap (4): when shops ____ big discounts.
questions.explanation: Shops 'offer discounts' to customers. Shops do not 'pay', 'spend' or 'earn' discounts; these verbs are used with money, not with discounts.
options: a) earn
b) offer
c) pay
d) spend

questions.question: Gap (5): let customers send items back free of ____.
questions.explanation: 'Free of charge' is a fixed expression meaning 'without paying'. 'Free of money', 'free of price' and 'free of value' are not used in English.
options: a) money
b) price
c) charge
d) value

questions.question: Gap (6): Whoever is right, one thing is ____: the way we shop has changed for ever.
questions.explanation: 'One thing is certain' means 'one thing is sure to be true'. 'Secure' and 'safe' describe things that are protected from danger, and 'confident' describes people, not facts.
options: a) certain
b) secure
c) safe
d) confident

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 6.
lesenParts.textTitle: From a village to the city
lesenParts.text:
Last year I left my small village in Wales and moved to Manchester to start my first job. I had never lived anywhere bigger (1) ______ our local market town, so I was quite nervous.

At first, everything felt strange. I was afraid (2) ______ getting lost, so I carried a map everywhere, and at night the noise of the traffic kept me awake. I didn't know anyone in the city, and neither (3) ______ my flatmate, who had just arrived from Spain. We spent most evenings watching television in our tiny kitchen.

Things got better when I found (4) ______ about a climbing club near my office. We went along together one evening, and now we go twice a week. Most of our friends here are people we met on the climbing wall.

These days I really enjoy city life. (5) ______ is always something to do, from free concerts in the park to street markets at the weekend. Rents are expensive, and I sometimes miss the quiet countryside. At (6) ______ same time, I can't imagine going back now. Moving to Manchester was one of the best decisions of my life.

questions.question: Gap (1): I had never lived anywhere bigger ____ our local market town.
questions.explanation: 'Bigger' is a comparative adjective, so it must be followed by 'than' before the thing it is compared with ('our local market town'). No other word can link a comparative to its second part.

questions.question: Gap (2): I was afraid ____ getting lost, so I carried a map everywhere.
questions.explanation: The adjective 'afraid' is followed by the preposition 'of' + noun or -ing form ('afraid of getting lost'). 'About', 'for' or 'to' do not work before 'getting' here.

questions.question: Gap (3): I didn't know anyone in the city, and neither ____ my flatmate.
questions.explanation: 'Neither + auxiliary + subject' means 'also not'. The first verb is in the past simple negative ('didn't know'), so the auxiliary must be 'did'. 'Was' or 'had' do not match 'didn't know'.

questions.question: Gap (4): Things got better when I found ____ about a climbing club near my office.
questions.explanation: 'Find out (about something)' is a phrasal verb meaning 'discover information'. Without 'out', 'found about' is not correct English.

questions.question: Gap (5): ____ is always something to do, from free concerts in the park to street markets.
questions.explanation: 'There is' introduces something that exists: 'There is always something to do'. 'It is always something to do' is not correct, because 'it' needs something to refer back to.

questions.question: Gap (6): At ____ same time, I can't imagine going back now.
questions.explanation: 'At the same time' is a fixed expression meaning 'but also / however'. 'Same' always takes 'the' in this phrase; 'a same time' or 'this same time' are not used.

Man: Would you like something to drink with your meal?
Woman: Yes, a fresh orange juice, please.
Man: I'm really sorry, but our juice machine isn't working today. We've only got apple juice in bottles.
Woman: Oh, I don't really like apple juice. I'll have a cup of tea, then. Actually, no, I'm so tired this morning. Could I have a coffee instead? A large one, please.
Man: Of course. Milk and sugar?
Woman: Just milk, thanks.

Man: Right, that's two large margherita pizzas. They're nine pounds each, so that comes to eighteen pounds.
Woman: Oh, isn't there a special offer on Tuesdays? The poster in the window says two pounds off.
Man: That's right, if you collect the order yourself.
Woman: Great. So that's sixteen pounds, then?
Man: Actually, it's two pounds off each pizza, not the whole order. So you only pay fourteen.
Woman: Even better! Here you are.
Man: Thanks. Enjoy your meal.

Mum: Hi, love. Did you manage to get everything on the list?
Girl: I think so. Here's the milk, and I got the big box of eggs, like you said.
Mum: Lovely, thanks. And the butter? I need it for the birthday cake this afternoon.
Girl: Oh no, I knew there was something. I was looking at the list on my phone and the battery died.
Mum: Never mind. Could you pop back to the shop for it? It's only five minutes away.
Girl: OK, I'll go now.

Man: Excuse me, are we too late for breakfast?
Woman: No, you're fine. From Monday to Friday we stop serving breakfast at eleven, but at weekends we carry on until half past eleven. And today's Saturday, so you've still got about twenty minutes.
Man: Oh, that's lucky.
Woman: Then we start the lunch menu at twelve o'clock, if you'd prefer something bigger.
Man: No, breakfast is perfect, thanks. Two full English, please.

Man: Shall we try that new Italian restaurant on the high street tonight?
Woman: I rang them this morning, actually. They're fully booked until Saturday.
Man: Oh, what a shame. Well, we could just cook something here instead.
Woman: There's nothing in the fridge, though, and I really don't want to go shopping now. What about the burger bar near the station? It's cheap, and you don't need to book.
Man: Good idea. I haven't been there for ages. Let's go at about seven.

Woman: That was delicious. What would you recommend for dessert?
Man: Well, the chocolate cake is the most popular, but to be honest it's quite heavy after a big meal like yours.
Woman: Mm, I am quite full. What about the fruit salad?
Man: It's fine, but it's nothing special. If I were you, I'd have the apple pie. Our chef makes it fresh every morning, and it comes with ice cream.
Woman: That sounds lovely. I'll try that, then.

Woman: Hi there, what can I get you?
Man: I was going to have the chicken salad, but it says on the board that it's finished.
Woman: Sorry, yes, we sold the last one about ten minutes ago. The soup of the day is still available, though. It's tomato, and it comes with fresh bread.
Man: Hmm, I had tomato soup at home last night, so I don't really fancy it again. I'll just have a cheese sandwich, please.
Woman: No problem. Brown or white bread?
Man: Brown, please.

Woman: Are you taking that jacket back to the shop? I thought you loved it.
Man: I do. The colour's great, and it fits me perfectly.
Woman: So what's the problem? Did you decide it was too expensive?
Man: No, it was actually in the sale, so it was a real bargain. But look at this. The zip's broken already, and I've only worn it twice.
Woman: Oh, that's annoying. Have you still got the receipt?
Man: Yes, luckily. I'm hoping they'll just give me a new one.

Man: Have you been to the new shopping centre yet?
Woman: Yes, I went on Saturday. Everyone told me it would be really crowded, but actually it was fine. I didn't have to queue anywhere.
Man: And what are the shops like?
Woman: Well, that's the thing. They're the same big chain stores you find in every town. I was hoping for some smaller, independent places, you know, something a bit different. So it was a bit disappointing, really.
Man: What about parking? That's always a nightmare in town.
Woman: Oh, that was great. It's free for the first three hours, and there were loads of spaces.

Woman: Did you see the post office has changed its opening hours? It's open until seven on weekdays now.
Man: Yes, I saw the notice.
Woman: Were you surprised?
Man: Not really. People had been asking for longer hours for ages. But it makes such a difference to me. I could never get there before five because of work, so I had to send all my parcels on Saturdays, and the queue was always awful.
Woman: I thought you'd be annoyed, because it's closed on Saturday afternoons now.
Man: That doesn't matter to me any more. I can just go on my way home.

Man: I really need a haircut, but I hated what the last place did to me.
Woman: You should try Sam's on Bridge Street. I've been going there for years.
Man: Is it cheap?

Man: Absolutely. They were the best thing there. That Thai curry I had was fantastic.

Presenter: And now some news for everyone who's planning to go to the Millbrook Summer Festival next weekend. As many of you know, for the last five years the festival has been held in the town square. This year, though, it's moving to Castle Park, because the organisers needed more space for all the new events.

The main stage won't be in the same place as before, either. Last year it was right next to the car park, and lots of people complained about the noise from the traffic. This time you'll find it next to the lake, which should be a lovely setting for the evening concerts.

There's plenty for younger visitors, too. Sadly, the painting competition won't be happening this year, but instead there's a cake decorating competition on Saturday afternoon for anyone under twelve. The winner gets a family ticket for next year's festival.

Now, a practical tip. There will only be a small number of chairs, and they're mainly for older visitors. So the organisers suggest that you bring a blanket to sit on. And please don't bring umbrellas, because they block the view for people behind you.

Tickets cost twelve pounds at the entrance, but if you buy them online before Thursday, you'll only pay eight pounds. Children under five get in free.

Finally, getting there. There's very little parking near Castle Park, and taxis will be expensive that weekend. So the best thing to do is to take the shuttle bus from the railway station. It runs every twenty minutes and it's free if you show your festival ticket.

So, that's everything for now. Have a great time at the festival!

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 4.
horenParts.transcript:
Interviewer: Today I'm talking to Lucy Grant, who has just been chosen for the national swimming team at the age of seventeen. Lucy, when did you first start swimming?
Lucy: I was seven. Everyone assumes I loved it from the very beginning, but actually I was terrified of putting my face in the water. My older brother was the keen one. I only went along because Mum didn't want to drive to the pool twice. The lessons themselves were fun, though. Our teacher turned everything into a game.

Interviewer: Now you train at five o'clock in the morning. That must be hard.
Lucy: People always say that's the worst part. And at first I hated hearing the alarm. But now I actually love it. The pool's really quiet, and I feel I've already achieved something before the day starts. My teachers used to ask if I fell asleep in class, but I'm more awake than anyone! What I find harder is the evenings, when my friends go out and I have to be in bed by nine.

Interviewer: You changed coaches two years ago. Why was that?
Lucy: My first coach was lovely, and she had loads of experience. The club was just round the corner from my house, too. But she mainly worked with sprinters, and I'd started to realise that I was better at longer races, like the eight hundred metres. So I joined a club that specialises in distance swimming. It means a longer journey, but it was the right decision.

Interviewer: Last year you didn't make the final at the national championships. How did you deal with that?
Lucy: Of course I was disappointed for a day or two. Some people said I'd been unlucky, because I had a cold that week, but that wasn't really it. When my coach and I watched the video, it was obvious that my starts were too slow. So we worked on them all winter. Looking back, it was the best thing that could have happened, because I'm much faster now.

Interviewer: You're quite popular on social media. How do you feel about that side of things?
Lucy: Some swimmers say it adds a lot of pressure, but I don't feel that at all. And I only post once a week, so it doesn't take up much time. The best thing is when girls send me messages saying they've joined a swimming club because they watched my videos. That makes it all worth it.

Interviewer: Finally, what advice would you give to young swimmers?
Lucy: Don't worry about finding the perfect club or buying expensive kit. And please don't compare yourself with other swimmers all the time. The most important thing is to make sure you're having fun. If you aren't enjoying it, you won't keep going when it gets difficult.
Interviewer: Lucy Grant, thank you very much.

schreibenParts.task:
You must answer this question. Write your answer in about 100 words.

Read this email from your English friend Sam and the notes you have made.

From: Sam
Subject: Your phone!

Hi,

Good news - I've found your phone! It was under the back seat of my car. You must have dropped it when I gave you a lift home from the cinema on Friday. [Note 1: Great! Thank Sam]

I can bring it round to your house, or you can come and pick it up from mine. Which would be better for you? [Note 2: Explain which and why]

I'm free on Saturday or Sunday this week. When shall we meet? [Note 3: Suggest a day and time]

By the way, how have you managed without your phone for the last few days? [Note 4: Tell Sam]

Sam

Write your email to Sam using all the notes.

Choose ONE of these questions. Write your answer in about 100 words.

Question 2 - Article
You see this notice on an English-language website for young people.

Articles wanted!
Technology in my life
What piece of technology do you use most, and what do you use it for?
Could you live without it for a week? Why or why not?
The best articles will be published on our website.

Write your article.

Question 3 - Story
Your English teacher has asked you to write a story.
Your story must begin with this sentence:
The phone rang at midnight.

Write your story.

sprechenParts.title: Part 1 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
Part 1 - Interview

The examiner asks you some questions about yourself. Answer each question with at least one or two full sentences.

1. What's your name? Where do you live?
2. What time do you usually get up on a weekday?
3. Tell us about what you usually do in the evenings.
4. What do you enjoy doing at the weekend?
5. Do you prefer spending your free time at home or going out? Why?
6. Tell us about something you did in your free time last week.

sprechenParts.title: Part 2 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
Part 2 - Photograph

Look at the photograph. It shows a group of people relaxing in a park on a sunny afternoon. In the front, a young family is having a picnic on a blanket under a large tree; a man is reading a book, and a little girl is eating a sandwich. Behind them, two teenagers are throwing a frisbee on the grass, and in the background an older woman is walking her dog along a path next to a small lake.

Tell us what you can see in the photograph. You have about one minute.

sprechenParts.title: Part 3 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
Part 3 - Collaborative task

I'm going to describe a situation to you. A group of friends has a free afternoon next Saturday. They want to do something together, but they don't have much money. Here are some things they could do.

go to the cinema
go for a bike ride in the countryside
play football or basketball in the park
cook a meal together at someone's house
visit a museum in the town centre

Talk together about the different things the friends could do, and say which would be the most enjoyable. Then decide which activity is the best for the group. You have about two or three minutes.

sprechenParts.title: Part 4 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
Part 4 - General conversation

Discuss these questions with your partner.

1. What free-time activities are popular with people of your age where you live?
2. Is there a free-time activity you don't enjoy? Why not?
3. Do you think people have less free time now than in the past? Why?
4. Would you like to try a new hobby? What would it be?
5. Is it better to spend free time with friends or on your own? Why?

items.signText: Sam, I'm at the shopping centre. The shoe shop you mentioned has closed down, but SportZone next to the cinema has a sale on trainers. Shall I buy the blue pair in your size now, or would you rather choose yourself on Saturday? Mum
items.question: Why is Sam's mum sending this message?
options: a) To find out where the shoe shop has moved to
b) To arrange to meet Sam at the cinema on Saturday
c) To ask if Sam wants her to buy some trainers today
items.explanation: Mum asks 'Shall I buy the blue pair in your size now, or would you rather choose yourself on Saturday?', so she wants to know if she should buy the trainers today. The shoe shop 'has closed down'; it has not moved. The cinema is only mentioned to say where SportZone is, and Saturday is when Sam might choose the shoes, not a meeting at the cinema.

items.signText:
CAR PARK
The first two hours are free if you show a receipt from any shop in the centre at the pay machine before you leave. Without a receipt, the normal charge of £2 per hour applies.
items.question: What does the sign say?
options: a) Parking is free for two hours with a shop receipt.
b) Anyone can park in the car park for two hours without paying.
c) Drivers have to pay at the machine as soon as they arrive.
items.explanation: The first two hours are free 'if you show a receipt from any shop in the centre', so only people who have bought something park for free. Without a receipt 'the normal charge of £2 per hour applies', so parking is not free for everyone, and the receipt is shown at the machine 'before you leave', not on arrival.

items.signText: Our bread is baked in store every morning. Anything left on the shelf at 6 p.m. is reduced to half price. Please note that reduced items cannot be put aside for customers to collect later.
items.question: What does the label tell customers?
options: a) The bread is baked fresh in the store twice a day.
b) Bread still on the shelf in the evening costs less.
c) Staff can keep cheaper bread for you to pick up later.
items.explanation: The label says 'Anything left on the shelf at 6 p.m. is reduced to half price', so bread bought in the evening is cheaper. Reduced items 'cannot be put aside for customers to collect later', so staff will not keep them for you, and the bread is baked 'every morning', not twice a day.

items.signText:
SELF-SERVICE TILLS 1–6: CARD PAYMENTS ONLY.
If you wish to pay with cash, please use the staffed tills near the main entrance. Staff at the customer desk can help with gift vouchers.
items.question: What does the notice say?
options: a) The self-service tills do not accept payment by card.
b) Customers paying with cash should go to the customer desk.
c) Customers who want to pay in cash must use a different till.
items.explanation: The notice says the self-service tills take 'card payments only' and that people who 'wish to pay with cash' should 'use the staffed tills near the main entrance', so cash customers need a different till. The customer desk is only mentioned for gift vouchers, not cash, and the self-service tills do accept cards — in fact they accept only cards.

items.signText:
TROLLEYS
You need a £1 coin to release a trolley. Your coin comes back when you return the trolley to any trolley park. Please do not take trolleys out of the car park.
items.question: What does the sign say about trolleys?
options: a) You may take a trolley home if you leave £1.
b) You will get your money back when you return the trolley.
c) You must return the trolley to the place where you got it.
items.explanation: The sign says 'Your coin comes back when you return the trolley', so you get your £1 back. Trolleys must not be taken 'out of the car park', so you cannot take one home, and you can return it 'to any trolley park', not only the one where you got it.

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 3.
lesenParts.textTitle: My summer with the sea turtles
lesenParts.text:
When I finished school last year, most of my friends went straight to university. I wasn't sure what I wanted to study, so I decided to spend three months as a volunteer on a sea turtle project on a small Greek island. My parents weren't very keen at first. They thought I should get a job and save money instead, but when I showed them that the organisation had been running for over twenty years, they began to feel more relaxed about it.

I arrived in June, just as the turtles were starting to lay their eggs on the beaches. There were about fifteen volunteers from all over the world, and we lived together at a simple campsite with tents and a shared kitchen. I'd never been camping before, and I'll be honest: the first week was hard. It was extremely hot, there were insects everywhere and I missed having my own room. But I soon got used to it, and by the end I actually preferred sleeping outside.

Our main job was to walk along the beaches early in the morning, looking for the tracks the turtles had left in the sand during the night. When we found a nest, we protected it with a metal cage so that dogs and foxes couldn't dig up the eggs. We also put up signs asking tourists not to use umbrellas or chairs near the nests. Most visitors were very interested and asked lots of questions, although a few were annoyed that part of the beach was closed.

What surprised me most was how much time we spent talking to people. Every evening, two volunteers ran an information stand in the harbour. I was terrified the first time because my Greek was limited to 'hello' and 'thank you', and many of the visitors were Greek families. However, the other volunteers helped me, and I learnt enough phrases to explain the basics. By August I was confident enough to give short talks to groups of children, which is something I would never have imagined doing a year earlier.

The best moment came near the end of my stay, when the first eggs hatched. Watching dozens of tiny turtles run across the sand towards the sea at midnight is something I will never forget. Only about one in a thousand will survive to become an adult, which made me realise why the project's work matters so much.

Looking back, I think the experience taught me more than any classroom could. I've now decided to study marine biology, and I'm hoping to return to the island next summer as a team leader. If you're thinking of volunteering, my advice is simple: don't choose a project just because it looks good in photos. Find out exactly what the work involves, and make sure it's something you really care about.

questions.question: Why did the writer's parents begin to feel better about her plan?
questions.explanation: The writer says that 'when I showed them that the organisation had been running for over twenty years, they began to feel more relaxed about it'. Her parents wanted her to 'get a job and save money instead', but she never promises to do this, and her friends 'went straight to university', not to the project.
options: a) Several of her friends were going on the same project.
b) She promised to find a job when she came back.
c) She had already saved enough money for the trip.
d) They learnt that the organisation had a long history.

questions.question: How did the writer feel about living at the campsite?
questions.explanation: She says 'the first week was hard', but 'I soon got used to it, and by the end I actually preferred sleeping outside'. She had 'never been camping before', so she was not camping again, and she says she soon got used to the conditions, so she did not miss her own room for the whole stay.
options: a) She never really got used to the heat and the insects.
b) She wished she had had her own room for the whole stay.
c) She found it difficult at first but later came to enjoy it.
d) She was pleased to be camping again after many years.

questions.question: What does the writer say about the tourists on the beaches?
questions.explanation: The writer says 'Most visitors were very interested and asked lots of questions'. Only 'a few were annoyed that part of the beach was closed', not most of them, and she never says that tourists damaged nests or ignored the signs.
options: a) Many of them wanted to find out more about the turtles.
b) Most of them were unhappy that some of the beach was closed.
c) They often damaged the nests with their chairs and umbrellas.
d) Very few of them paid attention to the volunteers' signs.

questions.question: Why was the writer frightened the first time she worked at the information stand?
questions.explanation: She was 'terrified the first time because my Greek was limited to "hello" and "thank you"'. She only gave talks to children later, 'by August', and 'the other volunteers helped me', so she was not left alone.
options: a) She had to give a talk to a large group of children.
b) The other volunteers had left her there on her own.
c) She did not know enough facts about sea turtles.
d) She could only say a few words in the local language.

questions.question: What advice does the writer give to people who are thinking of volunteering?
questions.explanation: Her advice is to 'Find out exactly what the work involves, and make sure it's something you really care about'. She warns people not to choose a project 'just because it looks good in photos', and she does not advise learning the language first or going with a friend.
options: a) Learn some of the local language before you leave.
b) Check carefully what you will be expected to do.
c) Go with a friend so that you do not feel lonely.
d) Choose a project in a place that looks beautiful.

lesenParts.text:
Twenty years ago, learning a new language or studying for a qualification usually meant sitting in a classroom at a fixed time each week. Today, millions of people learn at their kitchen table, on the bus or even in bed. (1) ______ In some countries, more than half of all adults have now taken at least one course on the internet.

There are several reasons for this growth. The most obvious is that the internet has become faster and cheaper, so watching video lessons is no longer a problem for most people. (2) ______ For example, a nurse who works nights can study during the day, while a parent can wait until the children are asleep.

Universities have also played a part. Many of them now put recordings of their lectures on the internet. (3) ______ Some of these have attracted over a million students, which would be impossible in any lecture hall.

However, online learning is not perfect. Many people sign up for a course with great enthusiasm but never finish it. (4) ______ Without a teacher checking their progress, they find it easy to put off the next lesson until tomorrow, and then the day after.

To solve this problem, many course designers now include ways for learners to stay in touch with each other. (5) ______ Students who feel part of a group, it seems, are much more likely to reach the end. In the future, the best courses may combine the freedom of learning online with the support that classrooms have always provided.

questions.question: Choose the sentence that best fits gap (1).
questions.explanation: 'Learning in this way' refers back to learning 'at their kitchen table, on the bus or even in bed', and the idea that it 'has become completely normal' is supported by the next sentence: 'more than half of all adults have now taken at least one course on the internet'. The sentence about printed textbooks is about paper books, so it breaks the link between these two sentences.
options: A) Some go even further and offer complete courses that anyone can join for free.
B) As a result, most online courses now cost more than they did ten years ago.
C) Learning in this way, once unusual, has become completely normal.
D) These include discussion forums, weekly video meetings and online study partners.
E) Because of this, schools no longer need to employ as many teachers.
F) Another reason is that online students can decide for themselves when to study.
G) Printed textbooks, however, are still more popular than ever.

The sentence saying courses 'cost more' contradicts 'faster and cheaper', and the one about schools needing fewer teachers is not what the nurse example shows.

Printed textbooks do not attract 'students' in a lecture hall, so that sentence cannot fit.

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 5.
lesenParts.text:
Last spring, our class went on a five-day trip to the mountains in Wales. We (1) ______ at a youth hostel in a small village, and every day our teachers organised a different activity. On the first morning we went climbing. I had never done it before, and at first I was too nervous to (2) ______ down, but our instructor was very patient. By lunchtime I had reached the top of the wall twice!

The next day we went on a long walk to a lake. The weather (3) ______ suddenly in the afternoon, and we got completely wet (4) ______ the way back. Luckily, the hostel staff had made hot soup for us, which warmed us up in no time.

In the evenings we played games and told stories. My best friend Leo, who is usually quite shy, (5) ______ everyone laugh with his funny impressions of our teachers. Fortunately, the teachers found them funny too!

I learnt a lot on the trip, not only about the mountains but also about working in a team. I would definitely (6) ______ it to next year's students.

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (1).
questions.explanation: 'We stayed at a youth hostel' is the normal way to say where you slept during a trip. 'Put', 'kept' and 'spent' all need an object (you put or keep something; you spend time or money), so 'We put/kept/spent at a youth hostel' is not correct.
options: a) put
b) kept
c) stayed
d) spent

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (2).
questions.explanation: When you point your eyes in a direction, the verb is 'look': 'too nervous to look down'. 'See', 'watch' and 'view' are not used with 'down' in this way.
options: a) watch
b) look
c) view
d) see

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (3).
questions.explanation: 'The weather changed suddenly' makes sense, and it explains why they 'got completely wet'. 'Became' and 'went' need a word after them (became cold, went grey), and weather does not 'move'.
options: a) changed
b) went
c) moved
d) became

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (4).
questions.explanation: The fixed phrase is 'on the way back', meaning during the journey back to the hostel. 'In the way' has a different meaning (blocking someone), and 'at the way' and 'by the way' do not mean 'during the journey'.
options: a) at
b) by
c) in
d) on

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (5).
questions.explanation: The structure is 'make someone do something': Leo 'made everyone laugh'. 'Caused' and 'got' need 'to' before the verb (caused/got everyone to laugh), and 'did everyone laugh' is not correct here.
options: a) made
b) did
c) caused
d) got

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (6).
questions.explanation: You 'recommend something to someone' when you say it is good: 'I would definitely recommend it to next year's students'. We 'advise' and 'persuade' people, not things ('advise it to' and 'persuade it to' are wrong), and 'tell it to' would mean repeating a story.
options: a) advise
b) recommend
c) tell
d) persuade

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 6.
lesenParts.textTitle: My summer as a camp leader
lesenParts.text:
Last summer I worked as a group leader at an adventure camp for teenagers in Scotland, and it was the best job I have (1) ______ had. I was responsible (2) ______ a group of twelve children aged between eleven and fourteen. Every morning I had to wake them up, make sure they ate a good breakfast and then take them to their activities, most (3) ______ which were outdoors. We went kayaking on the lake, climbed rocks and learnt how to build a fire safely.

The days were long and tiring. Some evenings I was (4) ______ exhausted that I fell asleep before the children did! The hardest part was looking after the ones who felt homesick. One boy, Callum, cried every night during his first week. I spent a lot of time talking to him and finding games he enjoyed, and by the end of the camp he was (5) ______ of the happiest children there.

I also made some great friends among the other leaders, and we still chat online most weeks. (6) ______ soon as applications open again, I'm going to apply for next summer.

questions.question: Write ONE word to fill gap (1).
questions.explanation: After a superlative with the present perfect we use 'ever': 'the best job I have ever had'. 'Never' would give the opposite meaning and is not possible after 'the best'.

questions.question: Write ONE word to fill gap (2).
questions.explanation: The adjective 'responsible' is always followed by 'for': 'I was responsible for a group of twelve children'.

questions.question: Write ONE word to fill gap (3).
questions.explanation: The relative phrase is 'most of which': 'their activities, most of which were outdoors', meaning that most of the activities took place outside.

questions.question: Write ONE word to fill gap (4).
questions.explanation: The structure 'so + adjective + that' shows a result: 'I was so exhausted that I fell asleep before the children did'. 'Such' is used before a noun, not an adjective alone, and 'too' cannot be followed by 'that'.

questions.question: Write ONE word to fill gap (5).
questions.explanation: 'One of the' is followed by a superlative and a plural noun: 'one of the happiest children'. By the end of the camp Callum was very happy, which contrasts with how he cried every night in his first week.

questions.question: Write ONE word to fill gap (6).
questions.explanation: The time expression is 'as soon as', meaning 'immediately when': 'As soon as applications open again, I'm going to apply'. No other word can come before 'soon as' here.

Girl: Hi Sam, it's Maya. It's about tomorrow. I know I said we'd meet at the ticket office, but it's always really crowded there in the morning. I thought about the café, but I've just remembered it's closed on Sundays. So let's meet under the big clock by the main entrance instead. It's easy to find. See you there at nine!

Woman: Hi Tom, it's me. I'm still at the station, and I'm afraid I'm going to be late. My train to York was supposed to leave at ten fifteen, but there's a problem with the signals. At first they said it would leave half an hour late, so at quarter to eleven. But they've just changed it again on the board, and now it says eleven o'clock. So I'll probably get to you around lunchtime. Sorry!

Driver: Good morning, everyone, and welcome aboard this coach to Edinburgh. The journey normally takes three hours, and that includes a short stop at a service station. But I'm afraid there are roadworks near Newcastle today, so we expect to arrive about half an hour later than usual. That means the whole trip will take around three and a half hours. Don't worry, though. Last winter, in the snow, it took us over four hours!

Woman: So, did you pack everything for your trip?
Man: I thought so. I checked my passport about three times, and I remembered to put my phone charger in at the last minute. But guess what? I left my sunglasses on the kitchen table! And it's supposed to be sunny all week.
Woman: Oh dear. Well, you can always buy some at the airport.
Man: I suppose so, but they're so expensive there.

Woman: A single to Cambridge, please.
Man: That's twelve pounds. Are you coming back today? Because an off-peak day return is only fourteen.
Woman: Oh, yes, I'm coming back this evening.
Man: Then the return is much better value. We also sell a weekly pass, but that's only worth it if you're travelling every day.
Woman: No, it's just today. I'll take the return, then.

Man: So how are you getting to the airport on Friday?
Woman: Well, I was going to take the bus because it's the cheapest, but it takes nearly two hours with all the stops. My brother offered to drive me, but his car's at the garage until next week. So in the end I've booked a seat on the train. It's only forty minutes, and the station is right next to the terminal.
Man: Sounds perfect.

Man: Excuse me, is this where the Oxford train goes from? Platform seven?
Woman: Well, it normally leaves from platform seven, but not today. They're doing some building work over there, so it's going from platform three instead.
Man: Three? Do I need to go over the bridge?
Woman: No, it's just past platform five, on this side. You can't miss it.
Man: Great, thanks very much.

Girl: Hi, Ben, it's Lucy. It's about tonight.
Boy: Hi, Lucy. Is everything OK?
Girl: Yes, but you know we were going to see the film at seven? I have to help my mum in the shop after work, so could we go to the nine o'clock one instead? Oh, and don't worry about your bike. My brother fixed mine yesterday, so I don't need to borrow it any more.
Boy: Nine's fine with me. See you at the cinema.

Boy: Are you coming on the trip to the science museum on Friday?
Girl: I have to. It's part of the course. I don't mind museums, and science is one of my favourite subjects, so that's not the problem.
Boy: Is it the early start? The coach leaves at seven.
Girl: No, that's fine. It's just that they've chosen the day of my swimming final. I've been training for months, and now I'm going to miss it. It's so unfair. Why couldn't they pick another day?

Man: Did you finish that crime series you were watching?
Woman: No, I stopped after four episodes.
Man: Oh? I thought the actors were supposed to be really good.
Woman: They were. The woman who played the detective was brilliant. And it wasn't about time. I was on holiday, so I had plenty of it. But there were so many characters, and it kept jumping backwards and forwards in time. By episode four, I had no idea what was going on, so I gave up.

Man: Is that your new phone? What do you think of it?
Woman: Well, it cost less than I expected because it was in the sale. And it's really simple to use. I set it up in five minutes. But the photos are nothing like the ones in the adverts. In the evening, they all come out dark and blurry.
Man: That's a shame. The camera was the main reason you chose it.
Woman: Exactly. I feel a bit let down, to be honest.

Woman: Have you been to that new café on Market Street yet?
Man: Yes, I went on Saturday with my sister. The cakes were lovely, and to be honest, the prices weren't bad for the size of them.
Woman: I heard it gets really busy.
Man: It was full, but they keep the music quiet, so we could chat easily. The problem was that we waited forty minutes for two coffees. There were only two people working there. I won't go back until they've got more staff.

Man: Since I started cycling to work, I feel so much fitter.
Woman: Me too. I sleep better, and I've got loads more energy. I'm not sure it saves me any money, though. I spent a fortune on the bike and all the clothes.
Man: Really? I think I save loads on petrol.
Woman: Maybe. And for me it's slower than the car. It takes me twice as long.
Man: Not for me. The traffic on my road is terrible in the mornings, so I get there much faster on my bike.

Coach: Good evening, everyone, and thanks for staying behind after training. I've got some exciting news about the club. As you know, we've been raising money for something new for over a year. A lot of you were hoping for a swimming pool, but I'm afraid that was far too expensive. Instead, we've built an indoor climbing wall, and it's ready to use from next week.

Now, if you've never climbed before, don't worry. We're running beginners' classes. We originally planned to have them on Tuesday evenings, but the hall is already busy then, so they'll be on Thursday evenings from seven till eight thirty.

What do you need? Well, you don't need to buy special shoes, because the club will lend you a pair, and we'll give you a helmet as well. But please bring your own water bottle. Climbing is hard work, and we can't sell drinks in the hall.

There's also a special offer. Last year new members got a free T-shirt, but this year anyone who joins before the end of May will get a free sports bag with the club logo on it.

To book a place on a class, you'll need to go to reception. We're hoping to add bookings to the website soon, but it isn't working properly yet, so please don't try that for now.

Finally, we need volunteers for July. The summer barbecue is already organised, thanks to the parents' committee, but we still need people to help with the fun run through the park. If you're free, please put your name on the list by the door. Thanks, everyone!

horenParts.transcript:
Interviewer: Today I'm talking to Helen Price, who works as a ranger in a national park in the north of England. Helen, why did you choose this job?
Helen: People often assume I wanted to escape the city, but actually I loved living in London. And the money certainly isn't the reason anyone becomes a ranger! No, it really goes back to when I was about ten. A ranger took our school group out at night to look for badgers, and I remember thinking, that's what I want to do when I grow up.
Interviewer: What's the hardest part of the job?
Helen: Everyone expects me to say the weather, but I've got good clothes, and I actually enjoy a stormy day. The hours can be long in summer, but I don't mind that either. What I find really difficult is when visitors leave rubbish or let their dogs chase the sheep, even though there are signs everywhere. I'm not comfortable telling people off, but sometimes I have to.
Interviewer: The park has had far more visitors in recent years. How do you feel about that?
Helen: Some of my colleagues worry about the paths getting damaged, but we've repaired most of them now, so I'm not too concerned. And the car parks get busy at weekends, but it's never really crowded up on the hills. Honestly, I'm delighted. So many people have discovered the outdoors, and that can only be a good thing.
Interviewer: Has technology changed your work?
Helen: A lot. We use cameras to count the animals, and there's an app for reporting problems like fallen trees. They save us loads of time, and they don't cost as much as people think. But a camera can't tell you why the deer have moved to a different valley. You still need someone who really knows the land.
Interviewer: What would you say to young people who'd like to do your job?
Helen: A degree can help, but it isn't essential. Some of the best rangers I know never went to university. Some people start by working in visitor centres, which is fine, but you don't learn much about the land there. The best thing is to volunteer. Parks are always looking for helpers, and it's the only way to find out if you really love the work.
Interviewer: And what about your own future?
Helen: I was offered a job training new rangers at our head office, but I turned it down. I'd be sitting at a desk all day. I did once think about working in a national park in Canada, but I'd miss this place too much. No, I'm happy right where I am, and I hope I'll still be here when I retire.

schreibenParts.task:
Read this email from your English-speaking friend Jamie and the notes you have made.

From: Jamie
Subject: My visit!

Hi!

Great news: I've booked my ticket, and I'm coming to stay with you for the weekend next month! [Note 1: Brilliant!]

I'll arrive on Friday evening. Is it better for me to get a taxi from the station to your house, or can you meet me? [Note 2: Explain]

What do you think we should do on Saturday? I'd love to see the best places in your town. [Note 3: Suggest...]

Also, what should I bring? I've no idea what the weather will be like. [Note 4: Tell Jamie]

See you soon,
Jamie

Write your email to Jamie using all the notes. Write about 100 words.

Choose ONE of these questions. Write your answer in about 100 words.

Question A: Article
You see this notice on an English-language website for young people.

Articles wanted!
A day out in my town
Where would you take a visitor for a perfect day out in your town? What would you do there, and why would they enjoy it?
The best articles will be published on our website.

Write your article.

Question B: Story
Your English teacher has asked you to write a story. Your story must begin with this sentence:

When I opened the door, my friend was standing there.

Write your story.

sprechenParts.title: Part 1 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
The examiner asks you some questions about yourself, travel and holidays. Answer each question with two or three sentences.

1. What's your name? Where do you live?
2. How do you usually travel to school or work?
3. Where did you go on your last holiday?
4. Do you prefer holidays by the sea or in the mountains? Why?
5. Tell us about a place in your country that you would like to visit.

sprechenParts.title: Part 2 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation: Look at the photograph. It shows a family on holiday in a small harbour town by the sea. There are colourful houses along the water, boats in the harbour, and the family is sitting at a table outside a café, looking at a map. Tell us what you can see in the photograph. You have about one minute.

sprechenParts.title: Part 3 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
Your class has won a prize: a one-day trip together. Here are some places you could go.

a city with museums and shops
a beach
a theme park
a national park for walking
a farm where you can help with the animals

Talk together about the different places and say which would be the most fun and interesting for the whole class. Then decide which place is best. You have about two or three minutes.

sprechenParts.title: Part 4 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
The examiner asks you and your partner some more questions about travelling. Give your opinion and reasons, and respond to what your partner says.

1. Do you prefer going on holiday with your family or with friends? Why?
2. Is it better to plan a trip carefully or to decide things when you get there?
3. What was the best trip you have ever been on? What made it special?
4. Do you think people should travel less by plane? Why or why not?
5. What can people learn from visiting other countries?

lesenParts.text:
We talked to sixteen-year-old runner Maya Lin about her life on and off the track. Maya recently won the national junior 800-metre championship, but she remains surprisingly down-to-earth.

Interviewer: Maya, congratulations on your gold medal! How did you first get into running?
Maya: Thanks! Actually, it was by accident. When I was eleven, my school's running team was short of one person for a relay race. The coach saw me running to catch the school bus and asked me to fill in. I didn't even have proper running shoes! I ended up running really fast, and the coach suggested I join the club. Before that, I preferred playing video games and reading. I never imagined I would become an athlete.

Interviewer: How do you manage to balance your training with your schoolwork?
Maya: It isn't easy. I train for about two hours every day after school, and more on weekends. I have to be very organized. I do my homework on the bus or during lunch breaks. My friends are very understanding, though they sometimes complain that I can't hang out with them on Friday nights because I have to sleep early for Saturday morning practice. But they always come to support me at my races, which means a lot.

Interviewer: Do you ever feel too much pressure before a big race?
Maya: Definitely. Before a race, my hands shake and I feel sick. But my coach taught me to view that nervous energy as a positive thing. She says it shows my body is preparing to run fast. Once the race starts, all the worry disappears and I just focus on my breathing and my steps. I don't think about winning; I just try to beat my own personal best time.

Interviewer: What are your goals for the future?
Maya: Of course, the Olympics is the ultimate dream, but that is a long way off. For now, I want to focus on my next race and keep improving. I also want to finish my school exams with good grades because education is important to me. If I have one piece of advice for other young people, it's to try new things. You might discover a talent you never knew you had!

questions.question: Why did Maya first start running?
questions.explanation: Maya explains that her coach saw her running to catch the school bus and asked her to fill in for a relay race because they were short of one person.
options: a) She wanted to get fit instead of playing video games.
b) Her school coach noticed her running for a bus.
c) She wanted to win a relay race for her school.

c) She regrets not having time to do homework with her friends.

questions.explanation: Maya says her coach taught her to view nervous energy as a positive thing, showing that her body is preparing to run fast.
options: a) It makes her perform worse than she should.
b) She has learned to use the feeling to help her run.
c) She tries to ignore it by thinking about winning.
d) It is something she only felt when she was younger.

questions.question: What is Maya's main priority for the near future?
questions.explanation: Maya states that she wants to focus on her next race and keep improving, but also finish her school exams with good grades because education is important to her.
options: a) Making sure she does well in both her sport and her studies
b) Finding a new coach to help her improve her times
c) Qualifying for the next Olympic Games
d) Encouraging other teenagers to take up running

questions.question: What would Maya write in a social media post to her followers?
questions.explanation: At the end of the text, Maya advises other young people to try new things because they might discover a talent they never knew they had, which matches option c.
options: a) "I'm so lucky my school coach forced me to run. Without her, I would still be playing video games all day."
b) "It's tough when you have to give up all your hobbies and friends for a gold medal, but it's worth it in the end!"
c) "Never be afraid to step out of your comfort zone. You might find a passion you didn't know existed, just like I did!"
d) "If you want to be a champion, you must ignore the pressure and only focus on beating the other runners."

lesenParts.textTitle: A Weekend at the Local Food Market
lesenParts.text:
Last Saturday, I decided to visit the local food market in the town centre. I had heard a lot about it from my neighbours, but I had never found the time to go before. [1] As soon as I arrived, I realized I should have come much sooner. The atmosphere was incredibly lively and full of energy.

There were dozens of colourful stalls selling everything from fresh fruit to homemade cakes. [2] The smell of freshly baked bread was particularly amazing, drawing a huge crowd to one corner. I spent about an hour just walking around and looking at all the delicious options.

What I liked most was talking to the people who worked there. [3] They were happy to explain how they made their cheese or where their vegetables were grown. This made the shopping experience feel much more personal than going to a normal supermarket.

By lunchtime, I was starting to feel quite hungry because of all the wonderful smells. [4] I chose a small stall selling traditional Spanish empanadas and sat on a wooden bench to eat them. They were absolutely delicious and very filling.

Before leaving, I bought some fresh pasta and a jar of local honey to take home. [5] I am already planning my next visit and cannot wait to try some of the other stalls.

lesenParts.text: Last July, my friends and I decided to (1) ______ the Green Valley Music Festival. It is one of the most popular outdoor events in the country, and it (2) ______ place every summer in a beautiful forest. We arrived early on Friday morning to set up our tent in the camping area. As soon as the music started, the atmosphere became absolutely (3) ______. There were several stages with different types of music, so there was always something great to listen to. We spent most of our time dancing and eating delicious local food from the stalls. Although it (4) ______ with rain on Saturday night, nobody seemed to mind. We just put on our raincoats and kept on singing. The organisers also handed out free hot drinks to everyone. It was an unforgettable weekend, and we have already (5) ______ to buy our tickets for next year. I would highly (6) ______ this festival to anyone who loves live music and nature.

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (1).
questions.explanation: 'Attend' is the correct verb to use when you go to an event like a festival, concert, or meeting. 'Assist' means to help, which does not fit the context.
options: a) invite
b) attend
c) assist
d) present

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (2).
questions.explanation: 'Takes place' is a common collocation meaning to happen or occur in a particular place.
options: a) gives
b) holds
c) takes
d) makes

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (3).
questions.explanation: 'Amazing' fits perfectly to describe an exciting and positive atmosphere. 'Pleased' and 'satisfied' describe how people feel, not the atmosphere itself.
options: a) pleased
b) amazing
c) satisfied
d) comfortable

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (4).
questions.explanation: The expression 'poured with rain' means it rained heavily. The other verbs do not collocate with 'with rain' in this way.
options: a) poured
b) fell
c) filled
d) dropped

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (5).

options: a) agreed
b) thought
c) offered
d) prepared

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (6).
questions.explanation: 'Highly recommend' is a very common collocation used to strongly suggest something to someone because it is good.
options: a) encourage
b) propose
c) advise
d) recommend

lesenParts.textTitle: A Family Trip to the Mountains
lesenParts.text:
Last weekend, my family and I went on a trip to the mountains. We decided to go [1] car because it was easier to carry all our bags. The journey took about three hours, and [2] the weather was a bit cloudy at first, it soon became sunny.

When we arrived, we stayed in a lovely wooden cabin [3] was located next to a beautiful lake. My father immediately suggested going for a walk. We walked [4] hours along the forest paths. We even saw some wild deer! Later, my younger brother and I spent the afternoon swimming in the cold, clear water of the lake.

In the evening, we cooked a delicious meal together. Then we all sat outside and looked at the thousands of bright stars above the quiet valley. It was [5] a wonderful experience that we have already decided to return next year. I am really looking forward [6] our next adventure in the mountains.

questions.question: Identify the missing word for gap [1].
questions.explanation: We use the preposition 'by' to talk about means of transport (by car, by train, by bus).

questions.question: Identify the missing word for gap [2].
questions.explanation: The conjunction 'although' (or 'though') is used to introduce a contrast between the cloudy weather and it becoming sunny.

questions.question: Identify the missing word for gap [3].
questions.explanation: We use the relative pronoun 'which' (or 'that') to refer back to a thing (the wooden cabin) in a relative clause.

questions.question: Identify the missing word for gap [4].
questions.explanation: The preposition 'for' is used to show a period of time (for hours).

questions.question: Identify the missing word for gap [5].
questions.explanation: We use 'such' before 'a/an + adjective + singular noun' to add emphasis to the statement.

questions.question: Identify the missing word for gap [6].
questions.explanation: The phrasal verb 'look forward to' always takes the preposition 'to' followed by a noun, pronoun, or gerund.

horenParts.transcript:
[Woman]: Did you go to the indoor climbing wall yesterday, Jack?
[Man]: I wanted to, but it was fully booked. My brother suggested going for a bike ride instead, but then his bicycle had a flat tire. So we ended up playing tennis at the local club.
[Woman]: At least you did some exercise!

[Man]: I need to get a birthday present for my sister. I was thinking of a silver necklace.
[Woman]: She doesn't really wear jewelry, does she? What about that book she wanted?
[Man]: Our parents already bought her that. I think I'll get her a nice wool scarf instead. It's getting cold now.
[Woman]: That's a lovely idea.

[Man]: I can't find my keys anywhere! I thought I left them on the kitchen table next to my wallet.
[Woman]: Did you check your coat pocket? You had them when we came inside.
[Man]: Yes, I checked. Oh, wait, I remember now. I put them down on the shelf by the front door when I was taking off my shoes.

Hello everyone, and thank you for joining our tour group today. I want to give you some practical information about our visit to the Science Museum tomorrow.

First, we will meet outside the main entrance at 8.45 am. Please don't be late as the bus leaves at exactly nine o'clock.

When we arrive, we will start our visit in the transport gallery on the ground floor. This is always very popular because of the old steam trains.

After that, you will have some free time. I highly recommend visiting the special exhibition on the first floor. It is about robots and how they are used in everyday life.

For lunch, you can eat your own sandwiches in the picnic area, which is next to the museum shop. Please do not eat inside the exhibition rooms.

In the afternoon, we have booked a special 3D film in the IMAX cinema. The film is about the history of space exploration. It starts at two-thirty and lasts for forty minutes.

Finally, before we go home, you can visit the gift shop. If you show your group ticket, you can get a discount on books and posters.

Are there any questions?

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 4.
horenParts.transcript:
Interviewer: Today I'm talking to Elena Rossi, a successful travel blogger. Elena, welcome. Why did you first start your blog, 'Elena's Footsteps'?

Elena: Well, I didn't plan to make it my job! I actually started it when I went on a gap year to South America. My parents were really worried, so I promised to write regular updates so they'd know I was safe. I didn't think anyone else would read it, but then other travelers started finding my posts and asking for advice.

Interviewer: That's amazing. You've been to so many countries. Which one stands out the most?

Elena: People always ask this! I love Japan for its food, and Iceland for the landscapes, but my absolute favorite was Albania. I didn't know much about it before going, but the local people were incredibly welcoming. One family even invited me into their home for dinner when I got lost. That kindness is what I remember most.

Interviewer: Traveling isn't always easy, though. How do you deal with things when they go wrong?

Elena: Oh, I've had missed flights, lost luggage, and food poisoning! At first, I used to get really stressed and angry. But I quickly realized that doesn't help. Now, I just accept that problems are part of the adventure. I try to stay calm and look for a solution, often by asking locals. They are usually happy to help a confused tourist.

Interviewer: You usually travel by yourself. Do you prefer that?

Elena: I do. When you travel with friends, you tend to stay in your own little bubble. But when you're on your own, you're forced to talk to strangers, which means you make new friends much faster. Of course, it can be lonely occasionally, but the freedom to decide where to go next without arguing is worth it.

Interviewer: What's the most challenging part of being a professional blogger?

Elena: People think it's a permanent holiday, but it's hard work. The toughest thing for me is the lack of a routine. I'm constantly moving, which makes it hard to exercise regularly or eat healthily. I don't mind the long hours spent editing photos or writing posts, because I love doing that, but not having a proper home base can be exhausting.

Interviewer: Finally, what tips do you have for someone wanting to start a travel blog?

Elena: Don't just write about the famous tourist spots that everyone knows. Try to find a unique angle. Write about your personal feelings and the small details, like the smell of a local market. And most importantly, write because you love it, not because you want to get free hotel rooms. Readers can tell if you aren't being genuine.

Interviewer: Thank you, Elena!

schreibenParts.task:
Read this email from your English-speaking friend Alex and the notes you have made.

***
From: Alex
Subject: Your new course!

Hi,

How are you? I heard you started a new course last week. What kind of course is it? [Tell Alex]

I'd love to know if you are enjoying it. Is the teacher nice? [Great!]

Maybe I can join you next time. When is the next class? [Answer]

Let's meet up this weekend to talk about it. Which day is better for you? [Suggest]

Write back soon,
Alex
***

Write your email to Alex using all the notes. You should write about 100 words.

Choose one of the following tasks (article or story). Write about 100 words.

Option 1: Article
You see this notice on an international English website for young people:

*Articles wanted!*
LEARNING SOMETHING NEW
What is a new skill you would like to learn? Why do you want to learn it? Is it easy or difficult for young people to learn new things?
Write an article answering these questions.

OR

Option 2: Story
Your English teacher has asked you to write a story. Your story must begin with this sentence:

*It was my first day at the class.*
Write your story.

lesenParts.text:
Moving to a new city is often described as an exciting adventure, but for me, it felt more like a challenge I wasn't ready for. Last summer, my parents announced that we were moving from our quiet village to the bustling city of Manchester. I had lived in the same house for fourteen years, and the thought of leaving my friends and my favourite local park was devastating.

When we first arrived, the noise was the biggest shock. Unlike the peaceful nights I was used to, the city never seemed to sleep. There were sirens, traffic, and people talking at all hours. For the first two weeks, I barely left my room. I felt like an outsider looking in, convinced that I would never fit into this fast-paced environment. I spent most of my time messaging my old friends, feeling sorry for myself.

However, everything changed when I joined a local photography club. I had always enjoyed taking pictures, and I thought it might be a good way to get out of the house. On my first day, I met a girl named Sarah who was also new to the area. We started exploring the city together, looking for interesting buildings and street art to photograph. Through her eyes, I began to see the city differently. Instead of just seeing traffic and noise, I started to notice the beautiful architecture and the vibrant culture.

It has been six months now, and I can honestly say I don't regret the move. While I still miss my old friends, I have built a new life here. I have learned that moving isn't just about changing your address; it is about changing your perspective. You have to be willing to step outside your comfort zone to find the hidden gems in any new place. If you are facing a big move, my advice is to find a hobby or a group that shares your interests. It makes the world feel a lot smaller and much friendlier.

It's magical. Interviewer: Any advice for beginners? Sarah: Be yourself. Don't try to copy other bloggers. Authenticity is what people want to see.

lesenParts.textTitle: Rising Star: An Interview with Leo Vance
lesenParts.text:
At just sixteen, Leo Vance has already made a name for himself in the world of competitive swimming. We caught up with him at his local training centre in Manchester. 'I started swimming when I was five,' Leo explains, drying off after a two-hour morning session. 'My parents took me to the pool every weekend, but I didn't really take it seriously until I joined a club at ten.'

Leo’s routine is demanding. He wakes up at 4:30 a.m. to be in the water by 5:15 a.m. 'It’s tough, especially in winter when it's dark and cold outside,' he admits. 'But when you’re in the pool, you forget the time. You just focus on your strokes.' Despite the hard work, Leo insists he has a normal social life. 'People think athletes don't have time for friends, but I make sure I see my mates on Friday nights. It’s important to switch off.'

His biggest challenge so far was the National Youth Championships last year. 'I was so nervous before the final race,' he recalls. 'I almost pulled out, but my coach reminded me why I started. I ended up winning silver.' That medal changed his perspective. 'It wasn't just about the prize; it was about proving to myself that I could handle the pressure.'

Looking ahead, Leo has his sights set on the international stage. 'The dream is the Olympics, obviously. But for now, I’m focused on improving my technique. My coach says I’m strong, but my turns need work.' When asked if he has any advice for other young athletes, he is humble. 'Don't let the sport define who you are. Enjoy it, work hard, but remember to have fun. If you stop enjoying it, you’ll never reach your potential.'

lesenParts.text:
Moving to a new city is often described as an exciting adventure, but for me, it felt more like a challenge I wasn't ready for. Last summer, my parents announced that we were moving from our quiet village to the bustling city of Manchester. I had lived in the same house for fourteen years, and the thought of leaving my friends and my favourite local park was devastating.

When we first arrived, the noise was the biggest shock. Unlike the peaceful nights I was used to, the city never seemed to sleep. There were sirens, traffic, and people talking at all hours. For the first two weeks, I barely left my room. I felt like an outsider looking in, convinced that I would never fit into this fast-paced environment. I spent most of my time messaging my old friends, feeling sorry for myself.

However, everything changed when I joined a local photography club. I had always enjoyed taking pictures, and I thought it might be a good way to get out of the house. On my first day, I met a girl named Sarah who was also new to the area. We started exploring the city together, looking for interesting buildings and street art to photograph. Through her eyes, I began to see the city differently. Instead of just seeing traffic and noise, I started to notice the beautiful architecture and the vibrant culture.

It has been six months now, and I can honestly say I don't regret the move. While I still miss my old friends, I have built a new life here. I have learned that moving isn't just about changing your address; it is about changing your perspective. You have to be willing to step outside your comfort zone to find the hidden gems in any new place. If you are facing a big move, my advice is to find a hobby or a group that shares your interests. It makes the world feel a lot smaller and much friendlier.
